d9a5df34a7dd9973: NEW YORK, Oct 24 — Oil prices rose to their highest levels since late April on Friday, with benchmark crude contract Brent North Sea climbing above US$116 (RM474) a barrel as the Middle East conflict raged on.
Global markets were contending “with concerns around surging oil prices and the sustainability of AI spending,” noted AJ Bell’s head of financial analysis Danni Hewson.

“Escalating tensions in Ukraine and the prospect of increased energy demand as the northern hemisphere heads into the winter months are only adding to the upwards pressure on oil and gas prices,” Hewson added.
The benchmark international oil contract, Brent crude for December, rose more than 3 per cent to US$116.72 (RM476.63) per barrel.
The benchmark US contract, West Texas Intermediate, jumped 3.8 per cent to US$103.27 (RM421.70) a barrel.
Wall Street’s main indices spent most of the day in negative territory. The Dow finished down 1.2 per cent, more than the 0.2 per cent retreat in the Nasdaq, reversing its trend in recent sessions.
“Today everyone appears to be rotating back into the stuff they rotated out of yesterday,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at online trading and investing platform IG.
“No one wants to be caught holding risk over the weekend,” he added.
European stock markets mostly dropped following some poorly-received earnings from Gucci parent Kering and Swedish group Volvo Cars.
Asian equity indices closed out the week mixed as technology companies managed to claw back some of the week’s hefty losses.

Rising energy prices have influenced movements across stock markets in recent days along with developments in the AI sector as investors have become more leery of massively expensive capital spending outlays for data centres.
“People are now looking at the cap ex as a liability and that’s different from six months ago,” said Joseph Zidle, chief market strategist at Cresset Capital.
Gucci, Volvo
Kering shed more than 16 per cent on Friday after the French luxury group published results that failed to reassure investors about a turnaround at its key Gucci brand.
Volvo Cars meanwhile plunged more than 24 per cent after it said US tariffs and strong competition from local brands in China pushed it into a third-quarter loss.
In response, the company announced a new five-billion-kronor (RM2.1 billion) savings plan it said would lead to about 2,000 job cuts in Sweden and 500 more globally.

Aside from energy markets, AI and earnings next week, focus will fall firmly on interest-rate meetings for the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank, as well as an update on US economic growth data. — AFP

558fcb3948ca1986: From the Tengku Ampuan of Pahang, Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah Before I begin, I would like to congratulate Muzium Negeri Pahang on its 50th anniversary, its Golden Jubilee.

On this occasion, I remember with gratitude my late father-in-law, Almarhum Sultan Haji Ahmad Shah, who made Istana Kota Beram available to become a museum. That decision gave our heritage a home, and the museum has come a very long way since then.
So has its director.

I still remember Dato' Farid, the Dato Setia Jasa, as a skinny young man, fresh out of university. To me, he was practically a little boy. Today, he has grown in experience, confidence and wisdom, and acquired a few white hairs along the way.
I hope the museum deserves most of the credit for his wisdom, and that I am not entirely responsible for the white hairs!
But seriously, Farid has grown with this museum. I congratulate him on the ideas, dedication and vision he has brought to it, and on the ideas and vision he continues to have.
Our museum is increasingly talked about, and that makes me proud.

A museum must keep moving. It should inform and welcome people. Its exhibitions should change, giving visitors something new to discover and a reason to return. It should attract families, students, scholars and people who may never have thought that a museum was a place for them.
It should make people feel that their history belongs to them.
That is what I believe Muzium Pahang has worked hard to achieve.
My thanks also go to the staff whose work makes all this possible, and to the Pahang State Government for understanding our ambitions and continuing to support us.
Although, with a self-confessed control freak as the museum’s royal patron, perhaps they have not always had much choice!

This is also where a royal consort has work to do. Alongside the Sultan’s responsibilities, there is a contribution we can make through supporting our heritage, encouraging its practitioners and helping ensure that what we have inherited reaches another generation.
For me, that work comes from love. Patronage means taking an interest, listening, learning and being willing to sit with the people doing the work. Sometimes, quite literally, on the floor.
To everyone who has helped this museum reach its Golden Jubilee, thank you.
I must also confess that I feel rather humbled standing before so many distinguished scholars, each a master in his or her field.
And yes, a little nervous.

This is a subject about which many of you have spent your professional lives thinking and writing. I come before you with my own experience, my research and a great love for what I have been studying.
I have also realised that this seminar is being conducted in Malay, and I have prepared my keynote in English.
I do have a Malay translation. But I find that the English version allows me to express some of these thoughts more naturally.
Dato' Farid once told me, “Tuanku, speak in your mother tongue.”
I told him, “Yes, that is exactly what I am doing. My mother is English!”

There are thoughts that come to me more readily in English, and others that find their expression in Malay. So please allow me to speak in the language in which I can best share these reflections with you. And if some Malay finds its way in, that too is part of how I think.
This seminar has a very special place in my heart because it concerns a subject that has become so important to me: the Hukum Kanun of the Malay world, our Laws.
Through the Hukum Kanun Pahang, I discovered history. But I also discovered something within myself.

It challenged me, gave direction to my curiosity and helped me recognise what I was capable of achieving through study. For me, the work I have done on the Hukum Kanun Pahang is my greatest personal achievement.
It has changed the way I see things.

These days, whatever I am watching, reading or discussing, I seem to find myself comparing it with the Hukum Kanun Pahang. My family must sometimes wonder whether I can still have a conversation without bringing it into the discussion.
But that is what happens when a subject takes hold of your mind and your heart. You begin to recognise connections you had not seen before.
I thank Allah for leading me to that discovery, and for the opportunity to learn from it.
The keynote I am about to share grew from one such connection.
Before Tun Abdul Razak Hussein became Prime Minister, he was already a Shahbandar.

Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah holds a master’s degree from the International Institute of Islamic Thought and Civilisation (ISTAC), International Islamic University Malaysia, and is currently a PhD candidate at ISTAC-IIUM.
189aa3c97594387f: KUALA LUMPUR: Although society has evolved, the fundamental role of a constitutional monarch remains unchanged, the Sultan of Selangor, Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah, said.
His Royal Highness said the Ruler had a responsibility to uphold the Constitution, preserve continuity and serve as a symbol of unity above political differences.

"The monarchy provides stability during times of change and reminds us that enduring institutions continue to play an important role in safeguarding national harmony," he said in a special interview in conjunction with his 25 years on the Selangor throne.
Sultan Sharafuddin said the Constitution provided clear guidance on his responsibilities.
"My responsibility is to serve all the people of Selangor without favour or prejudice," he said.

His Royal Highness noted that respect for constitutional principles, impartiality and fairness enabled the monarchy to remain a trusted institution for all citizens, regardless of their background or political beliefs.
The monarchy, he said, represented continuity, stability, service and responsibility.
"It reminds us that leadership carries obligations rather than privileges," His Highness said.
Sultan Sharafuddin said these values remained relevant because societies benefited from institutions that encouraged moderation, unity and respect for the rule of law.
2812c96caca1932b: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 24 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has highlighted the need for Cabinet members to look at major policy shifts required to strengthen national resilience in industry and the economy.
He said he had raised the matter with cabinet members earlier today, emphasising that Malaysia has the resources, human capital, discipline, and resilience.
Anwar said he remained optimistic that Malaysia could forge ahead as a great nation through continued efforts by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (MITI) and collaboration with industry.
He was speaking at the Majlis Anugerah Kecemerlangan Industri (AKI) 2026 at Menara MITI here yesterday.
Also present were Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani and Deputy Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Sim Tze Tzin.
Anwar, who is also finance minister, said the government played a pivotal role in ensuring stability and confidently crafting economic and national policies.
He cited the New Industrial Master Plan, energy transition, and digital transformation, stressing that policy clarity must be matched by effective execution.
“And in most countries, they can introduce and come up with some impressive plans, but there is no certainty that you are able or you will be able to execute it effectively.
“So the role of not only bureaucracy, but more so the industrial players, is critical,” he added. — Bernama
5ba1d2ed8781df53: OCTOBER 24 — Say what you want about James Gunn’s reign as the CEO of DC Studios, but you certainly can’t say that he’s been boring, that he hasn’t tried enough new things, or that he’s played things safe.

In an era where comic book cinema has routinely felt like a corporate conveyor belt running on autopilot, Gunn’s tenure has at least injected an unpredictable, auteur-driven ambition into a studio that desperately needed a shot in the arm.
Sure, the distinctly average Supergirl might stand as the only real blip in his reign so far, a film that stumbled into the same safe, paint by numbers studio traps we’ve grown so weary of.
But the arrival of the hugely refreshing Clayface is more than enough to make DC fans hope again.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

(From left) Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries, English actor Naomi Ackie and English actor Max Minghella pose on the red carpet upon arrival to attend the European Premiere of ‘Clayface’ at Curzon Mayfair in London October 20, 2026. — AFP pic
It is a bold, uncompromising entry that proves there is still life left in comic book adaptations if you know how to break the mold.

I’ve always said that we’ve been nearing an absolute saturation point for superhero and comic book movies for a while now. Because let’s face it, there are only so many times we can slog through another standard superhero or supervillain origin story without starting to get bored out of our minds.

We know the plot beats by heart, the tragic backstory, the lab accident or ancient artifact, the montage of discovering new powers, and the inevitable third-act CGI punch-fest in a ruined city square.
And I’ve also always maintained that Marvel’s smartest tactical move to sidestep this saturation point was making films that sat firmly outside the traditional superhero genre.
Spider-Man: Homecoming wasn’t just a superhero flick, it was a John Hughes-style teen high school comedy that happened to feature Peter Parker.

Spider-Man: Far From Home was essentially a rowdy European student trip movie wearing an MCU suit. By smuggling comic book icons into established, functional film genres, you give the audience a fresh reason to care.
It looks like Gunn has brought that exact same philosophy over to DC with Clayface.

Yes, on paper, this is a supervillain origin story very much in the vein of Joker. But instead of cosplaying as a gritty, Martin Scorsese-homaging crime drama, Clayface is presented unabashedly as a full blown body horror flick.

To prove they weren’t messing around, DC brought in a legit horror director to steer the ship; James Watkins, the British filmmaker behind modern genre standouts like Eden Lake, The Woman in Black, and the recent American remake of Speak No Evil.
And who did they bring in to write the script? It’s Mike Flanagan, who’s responsible for recent horror favourites like The Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass, Oculus, Hush and Doctor Sleep.

Watkins brings a dark, deeply uncomfortable sense of psychological dread to the narrative, which centres on washed-up young actor Matt Hagen, whose fame and fortune was cruelly taken away from him in a tragic display of stupidity that could happen to even the best of us.
Desperate to reclaim his good looks, stardom, and place in Hollywood, Hagen turns to an experimental, not-yet-approved-for-human-testing technology that promises to restore his face.
Naturally, the side effects are grotesque, and Hagen’s mind degrades alongside his liquefying anatomy.
What makes the film work so remarkably well is its thematic DNA. I really enjoyed the movie’s brilliant blend of Obsession, The Substance, and Brian Yuzna’s 1989 cult classic Society.
Like The Substance, it takes Hollywood’s toxic, ageist obsession with physical perfection and turns it into a gory, sickening farce.
But it also channels the tragic, flesh-warping tragedy of David Cronenberg’s The Fly.

Much like Jeff Goldblum’s Seth Brundle watching his own physical decay in horrified fascination, Hagen’s descent isn’t just a visual nightmare, it’s also a heartbreaking character study of a man losing his humanity and mind to his own vanity.
Visually, the film is a total triumph for practical and practical-adjacent genre fans.
The yucky, gooey special effects deserve special praise here. The sheer texture of Hagen’s dripping, shifting, and melting flesh feels horribly tactile.

It is the kind of skin-crawling, stomach-churning visual work, echoing Cronenberg’s finest biological horrors, that would absolutely belong in a hard R-rated horror flick, far away from the sanitised, plastic CG gloss we usually get in modern studio blockbusters.
Every time Hagen tries to mold his face back into shape, the wet squelches and tearing tissue make you squirm in your seat.

If I had to rate it, Clayface is a solid 7 or 8 out of 10 movie, a gripping, tragic, and genuinely terrifying ride that takes a classic Batman villain and treats his tragedy with real genre reverence.

By refusing to deliver a comfortable, toy commercial origin story and instead handing the reins to a seasoned horror director, DC has delivered one of the most delightful cinematic surprises of the year.
It proves that when you stop treating comic book properties as rigid franchises and start treating them as versatile canvases for distinct genres, the multiplex can still be a thrilling place to be.
* This is the personal opinion of the columnist.
baa649ff164e729b: AMMAN, Oct 24 — Gunmen killed at least seven people and wounded dozens at a church in southern Jordan on Friday, with the king vowing retaliation for the rare attack on Christians in the majority Sunni Muslim kingdom.
Assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate and opened fire, authorities said.
The gunmen got out of a vehicle and started shooting during a funeral procession, the public security directorate said in a statement, adding that a hunt was underway for the perpetrators.
“The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation,” King Abdullah II said in an English-language post on X.
“We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation.”
After authorities gave a death toll of six, Director of Public Security Major General Abdullah Al-Maaytah said it had risen to seven with 34 injured, 27 of whom were still receiving treatment.
Images from state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka showed the king visiting Karak on Friday evening after the attack.
The Royal Court also shared a video showing the monarch at a local hospital in military uniform to check on the wounded.
“This country is ours and we will not abandon it — we will never abandon it,” an injured man told him.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

King Abdullah II (centre) speaks to one of the people injured at the Prince Ali Military Hospital in Karak, Jordan after gunmen attacked a church during a funeral on October 23, 2026. — Jordanian Royal Palace handout pic via AFP
Footage aired by Al-Mamlaka also showed the moment of the attack.
Two gunmen are seen dressed in casual clothes and brandishing pistols, with a third carrying a long gun, before they open fire on the church from an entrance on the street and charge forwards.

“A terrorist group has carried out a horrific act, one that is condemned in every respect, and the security services are working round the clock to track them down,” Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya told a press conference.
“Jordan has been targeted by a terrorist attack carried out by a group of extremists.”
He said the perpetrators had “absolutely no connection whatsoever to human values” and it “only serves to strengthen the Jordanians’ resolve... to combat and fight terrorism in all its forms”.

Mohammed Al-Khalayleh, minister of awqaf, Islamic affairs and holy sites, said “the sanctity of places of worship is inviolable and any violation of this is unacceptable on religious, moral and national grounds”, calling national unity “a red line that must not be crossed”.
Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered a three-day period of national mourning from Friday, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.
‘Heinous’
Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.
A witness told Al-Mamlaka the gunmen fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.
Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding that most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Screen grab from CCTV footage aired by Al-Mamlaka shows the moment gunmen attacked a Greek Orthodox church in Hammoud, Karak governorate, on October 23, 2026. — Al Mamlaka TV pic via AFP
Karak is home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up between two and three per cent of the population.
The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese in Jordan said that if the attack was aimed at driving out Christians from the holy land, “it will only make us cling to it more firmly and deepen our roots in it”.

“We are absolutely certain that Jordanian society will remain impervious to every dark, extremist ideology, and that this criminal act is far removed from – and alien to – the moderate Islam of our country,” it said.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, the Arab world’s only Christian head of state, called the shooting a “heinous terrorist attack”.
He said it “reaffirms once again that terrorism has no religion and no homeland, and its aim is to strike at coexistence and spread strife”, according to a presidency statement.
A spokesman for UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said “an attack not only on a place of worship, but during a funeral procession, is especially heinous”.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis also condemned the attack, saying on X that targeting a place of worship was “an affront to our shared humanity”.
Attacks on houses of worship in Jordan are rare.
In 2016 an attack in Karak targeted a security centre and police patrols, leaving 10 people dead.
The victims included seven security personnel and a female tourist, before four militants who had barricaded themselves inside Karak’s historic castle were killed. — AFP

* Editor’s note: Awqaf is the Arabic plural of waqf, an Islamic endowment, meaning property or assets donated and held in perpetuity for religious or charitable purposes. In Jordan, the Ministry of Awqaf, Islamic Affairs and Holy Sites oversees mosques, religious affairs and the management of such endowments.

69e2ba331d6aa502: KUALA LUMPUR: The Sultan of Selangor has credited the people of the state for making his 25 years as ruler a successful and meaningful journey.
His Royal Highness Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah said Selangor had remained one of the country's most important states, thanks to the contributions of its people and those who had made it their home.
"This would not have been possible without the role of Selangorians and the millions from other states who work here and make Selangor their home.
"I am thankful and proud to have been the ruler of this state over the past 25 years and Raja Muda for 33 years," he said, expressing gratitude to Allah for granting him good health.

Reflecting on his reign, Sultan Sharafuddin said every year had brought its own challenges and blessings, but the most meaningful moments had been those spent meeting the people of Selangor, celebrating their successes and standing alongside them during difficult times.

"I have witnessed our state continue to grow into one of the nation's leading centres of commerce, education and innovation, while maintaining its cultural and religious heritage," he said in an interview in conjunction with his Silver Jubilee celebrations.
His Royal Highness said he treasured seeing young people of all races excel, communities unite in times of adversity, and institutions work together for the betterment of society.
"These are reminders that the true strength of Selangor lies not only in its economy but also in its people," he said.
Asked how his understanding of leadership had evolved since ascending the throne, Sultan Sharafuddin said leadership was ultimately about responsibility and service.

"Over the years, I have come to appreciate even more deeply that a ruler must listen carefully before making judgments, remain calm during uncertainty, and always place the interests of the people above all else.

"Experience has taught me that leadership requires consistency, patience and humility. A ruler's responsibility is not merely to respond to the present but also to safeguard the future for generations to come," he said.
Sultan Sharafuddin said Selangor had continued to strengthen its position as Malaysia's economic engine while expanding opportunities in education, healthcare, infrastructure and investment.
"But we must not rest on our laurels. Other states, such as Johor and Penang, have become competitors too, but that is good and healthy," he said.
However, he expressed dissatisfaction that basic problems, particularly flooding and cleanliness, remained unresolved.

"Simple matters like floods and cleanliness remain unresolved, which makes me unhappy," he said, adding that he continued to receive complaints about poor rubbish collection, inadequate maintenance of cleanliness and flooding.
The ruler said the public often sent him complaints directly, complete with their personal details and photographs, which he would then forward to the menteri besar's office.
Sultan Sharafuddin said preserving harmony among Selangor's diverse communities was equally important.

"Economic success is meaningful only when it translates into better lives for ordinary citizens. Progress should always be measured not simply by numbers, but by the well-being, dignity and opportunities enjoyed by the people," he said.
9388c412367c7075: KUALA LUMPUR: Seremban recorded the country's highest Air Pollutant Index (API) reading at 169 as of 8am today, with unhealthy air quality also recorded in several other areas.
Bandaraya Melaka recorded an API reading of 163, while Batu Muda in Kuala Lumpur and Bukit Rambai in Melaka registered 162 each.
Batu Pahat and Pasir Gudang in Johor also recorded 162, while Tangkak registered 161.

Other areas with unhealthy air quality included Kluang (158), Alor Gajah and Pengerang (156 each), Segamat (155), IPD Serian in Sarawak (153), Cheras in Kuala Lumpur, Port Dickson in Negri Sembilan and Sri Aman in Sarawak (152 each), and Putrajaya and Kapit in Sarawak (151 each).
Petaling Jaya and Klang in Selangor recorded API readings of 133 and 121 respectively.

Meanwhile, Langkawi in Kedah recorded an API reading of 50, followed by Kangar in Perlis (48), Kota Baru in Kelantan (45), Kuala Terengganu in Terengganu (44), Tanah Merah in Kelantan (39) and Besut in Terengganu (25).
The Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS) also reported moderate air quality at 41 monitoring stations nationwide.
An API reading of 0 to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, and 301 and above hazardous.
d0fedea3069220c8: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 24 — Budget 2027 provides a comprehensive framework to empower young people by expanding access to quality job opportunities, industry-driven skills training and stronger social protection.

Perdana Fellows Alumni Association secretary-general Amir Izzwan Abu Hasan said the budget initiatives covered various key stages of youth development, helping young people build resilience in the face of current economic challenges.

He said one of the major initiatives that should be fully utilised was the RM8 billion allocation to strengthen the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) ecosystem, alongside access to 16,000 courses on the Coursera platform and 100,000 free subscriptions to artificial intelligence (AI) technology.
“These funds and facilities provide an excellent platform for young people to upskill and reskill, ensuring their skills meet current industry demands.

“The MADANI Talent Programme, which aims to create 30,000 high-quality job opportunities by 2027, also reflects the government’s emphasis on quality employment that offers progressive wages, social protection and clear career pathways,” he said when appearing as a guest on Bernama TV’s Darah Muda programme titled Budget 2027: How Much Will Youth Benefit? Tonight.

Elaborating further, Amir Izzwan said young people should also take full advantage of wage restructuring policies, particularly the increase in the minimum wage to RM2,000, scheduled to take effect in June 2027.

He also described the relaxed deferment terms for National Higher Education Fund Corporation (PTPTN) loan repayments, along with discounts for consistent repayments, as much-needed financial relief that would help them manage their daily cash flow.
For gig economy workers, he said the expanded RM160 million support package and the Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) aid should be fully utilised to cope with the rising cost of living.

He also suggested exploring additional initiatives, such as affordable rental housing near public transport facilities and the expansion of the My50 travel pass, to ease the daily financial burden on urban youth.

“If opportunities are available but young people themselves are not proactive in seizing them, they will go to waste. Young people must make the most of these opportunities to advance their careers and improve their standard of living,” he said. — Bernama
2fbace6fbec50439: KUALA LUMPUR: The Sultan of Selangor hopes future generations of Selangorians will be knowledgeable, compassionate, resilient, united and respectful of others.
His Royal Highness Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah said young people should strive for excellence without losing their sense of responsibility towards society.

"They should also understand that diversity is one of Malaysia's greatest strengths. Mutual respect and understanding will remain essential to our continued harmony and progress," he said in a special interview held in conjunction with his Silver Jubilee celebrations.
The Selangor ruler also advised young people to read news reports in depth before commenting, particularly on social media, rather than forming opinions based solely on headlines.
Sultan Sharafuddin said the younger generation had rightly placed importance on environmental sustainability and heritage preservation.
"Economic progress should never come at the expense of our natural environment or historical identity.

"Planning for future generations means protecting forests, rivers and green spaces while preserving our historical landmarks and cultural traditions. Development and conservation are not opposing goals; they should reinforce one another," he said.
His Royal Highness also noted that education remained the foundation of long-term progress, particularly in preparing young people for a rapidly changing world.
"Artificial intelligence may not replace all jobs, but in many instances, people who are trained in AI will replace those who are not.
"Selangor must not lose out in this area. We must be ready for this, and I hope the state government realises it," he said.
Sultan Sharafuddin also cautioned that the well-being of senior citizens must not be overlooked as Selangor moves towards becoming an ageing society.
The Sultan said healthcare services must evolve alongside demographic changes, while innovation should continue to strengthen the state's competitiveness.

His Royal Highness proposed that Selangor strive to become the first state to establish a dedicated geriatric medical centre specialising in the health, care, prevention and treatment of conditions affecting older adults.
These include age-related problems such as falls, frailty, urinary incontinence and memory decline.
"We need to prioritise the overall quality of life of the elderly, including their safety, independence and balanced medication," he added.

d0083dff0b0e337e: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 24 — You can always escape the chaos of the city, even if you don’t actually leave it.
No, you don’t have to check into a hotel and hole yourself up in your room (this sounds worse than any metropolitan mayhem, to be honest).
Instead, consider simply going out for a coffee. Not in a mall but in a café that feels more like somebody’s home.
With this plan in mind, we head to Gong Dou Coffee, located along the time-worn Jalan Goh Boon Hong in Taman Taynton View, Cheras.

With its cosy charms — thanks in part to exuberant, lush greenery contrasting with blackened, reclaimed wood for a lived-in ambience — Gong Dou promises a truly bucolic getaway in the heart of the city.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Barista making coffee with direct fire roasted beans. — Picture by CK Lim
The barista comes over with their coffee menu, explaining the provenance and profile of each varietal.
This is a common enough experience in most cafés serving specialty coffee nowadays, but Gong Dou stands out by using direct fire roasted beans.
To be exact, direct fire roasted beans from YiLuDou, a micro coffee roastery, which is just downstairs from Gong Dou.
After all, Jalan Goh Boon Hong is known for its iconic row of garage and mezzanine duplexes; recent gentrification meant that a number have been revamped into cafés.

That motif of the direct fire roasting extends to their revamped décor (consider Gong Dou Coffee a reinvention of Ah Gong House, its former incarnation in the same space), where choice accents are the result of yakisugi, a traditional Japanese technique for charring the surface of timber to protect it from the elements.
Instead of tracking down a Japanese yakisugi artisan, that owner Lois Loo had a woodworking friend of hers successfully replicate the process on the premises (outside, of course). Impressive!
Such attention to detail meant that we had high hopes for their curated selection of coffee beans too; we chose two, one natural processed and one washed.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Ethiopia Oromia Shakiso Hangadhi G1 as pour-over coffee. — Picture by CK Lim
First, for our pour-over coffee, we went with their Ethiopia Oromia Shakiso Hangadhi G1. Bright and expressive, the natural process gave the cup a gentle wine-like sweetness.
As it cools, the fruit becomes more apparent: dried blueberry initially, followed by a darker cacao note. Light-bodied and clean, yet with enough complexity without being too syrupy.
This is exactly our style of pour-over brew, the sort you drink slowly, allowing the temperature change to bring out different flavours with each sip.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Milk coffee made with Colombia Finca Manantiales del Frontino Geisha. — Picture by CK Lim
To switch things up, we also ordered a milk coffee. Rather than a safe, balanced blend, we opted for their Colombia Finca Manantiales del Frontino Geisha.

Some might argue using this premium bean, with its limited availability, for a milk coffee to be a bit of a waste. Ah, but if it’s made properly, you can enjoy its delicate floral character with a creamier finish.
Hints of elderflower appear alongside a bright, pomegranate-like fruitiness. The fully washed process ensures a clean, sweet and fragrant cup, avoiding the pitfall of heavier fermented flavours.
Beyond coffee (and some non-coffee beverages such as matcha and 21-year aged pu-er), their small menu is split between brunch fare and teatime treats.

The former features homemade quiches with fillings such as salmon and spinach, organic broccoli and mushrooms, as well as an Osaka inspired okonomiyaki quiche, topped with shaved katsuobushi (dried bonito flakes).
Given it was already afternoon, we leaned towards the latter with baked offerings ranging from passion fruit cheesecake to a heady mochi tiramisu, infused with Kahlúa and rum.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Strawberry ‘mochi’. — Picture by CK Lim

Mochi sounded good but we didn’t really feel like a boozy hit with our Japanese rice cake. Instead we opted for their strawberry mochi. Topped with a whole strawberry, this handmade pastry was surprisingly generously sized.

The fruit itself is juicy and nicely chilled, which pairs well with the chewy mochi skin. Simple but balanced, with just enough sweetness in the soft rice dough without overwhelming the natural flavour of the strawberry.
We also shared a slice of coffee nut tart; having eschewed the coffee liqueur of the mochi tiramisu, we still wanted a dessert with some serious caffeine kick to it.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Coffee nut tart. — Picture by CK Lim
This tart has a biscuity, cake-like base, with a craggy edge that reminds us of an apple crumble. The filling is a layer of chopped hazelnuts brushed thickly with a sticky espresso glaze.
The espresso comes through clearly with every bite; expect a deep coffee aroma and a subtly nutty, roasted note that prevents the tart from tasting too rich or sweet. A confident, adult pastry, this.

You could lose track of time lingering over your coffee here, eyes wandering from the pots of slender fiddle-leaf figs that stretch towards the patio ceiling or the unruly mass of blue pea flowers in one corner of their verdant, tropical garden.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Part of the verdant, tropical garden. — Picture by CK Lim
As promised, a proper getaway in the heart of the city. Less of an escape though; perhaps, more of a discovery? And a fine one at that.

24cb6a78db272a6f: GENEVA, Oct 24 — The Ebola patient in Nigeria is a Swiss woman, and the wife of a staff member at Switzerland’s embassy in Abuja, Bern said Friday.
The couple had recently travelled together to Uganda, but neither of them had visited the Democratic Republic of Congo — the epicentre of the current outbreak, the Swiss foreign ministry said.
On Tuesday, Nigeria announced its first recorded Ebola case, saying it was a woman who arrived in Abuja on a flight from Uganda. A total of 44 contacts have been identified.

On Wednesday, the authorities confirmed that the patient had the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is driving the outbreak in the DRC and for which there are currently no specific vaccines or treatments.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry said Friday she was “the wife of a Swiss member of staff” at Bern’s embassy in the Nigerian capital Abuja.
“The Swiss woman, who is symptomatic, has been hospitalised for about a week at a private clinic in Abuja,” it said in a statement.
“The infection may have occurred during a trip to Uganda approximately two weeks ago,” the Swiss authorities added.
“Her husband is in isolation; he has shown no symptoms. He accompanied his wife on the trip, during which she is believed to have contracted the Ebola virus,” it said.
“Neither individual travelled” to the DRC, it added.
The ministry said that the 25 other embassy staff members – eight Swiss nationals and 17 local employees – “are also doing well”.
Following consultations with the Nigerian health ministry and the World Health Organization (WHO), they do not need to go into isolation, the statement said.
Bern is considering the “potential repatriation of the patient” to Switzerland, it added.
The WHO said the patient developed symptoms on October 7, four days after arriving in Nigeria; sought care in Abuja on October 11; before testing positive for Bundibugyo on October 20.

“National authorities, with support from WHO and partners, have intensified contact tracing, case investigation and infection prevention and control measures, including the provision of essential supplies and personal protective equipment for health workers,” the UN health agency said in an update.
“Investigations are ongoing to establish the likely source of infection and reconstruct the travel and exposure history.
“WHO advises against any restriction of travel to, or trade with, affected countries,” it added.
Following the DRC, Uganda and Kenya, Nigeria has become the fourth African country to be affected by the Bundibugyo outbreak, which flared up in northeastern DRC in May. — AFP

c1b73c72abf49579: SINGAPORE, Oct 24 — Singapore expanded on Friday its probe into companies linked to fires in Indonesia, asking 10 locally-based firms for information about their efforts to contain blazes blamed for toxic haze covering the region.

The city-state has beefed up measures to combat the months-long blazes and had vowed legal action against companies responsible for the fires that have made regional air quality among the world’s worst.

Over the past week, Singapore issued notices to 10 foreign-based companies, insisting that they deploy fire fighting teams, stop burning or starting new fires in Indonesia and submit information about their links with associated companies in Indonesia and Singapore.
The information is to be reviewed by Singapore’s National Environmental Agency (NEA).

In addition to these companies, the NEA is seeking information from 10 Singapore-registered firms in the palm oil or forestry industry who are involved with Indonesian land, the environmental agency said in a statement late Friday.

The information relates to “linkages with associated companies in Singapore and Indonesia, the location of land concessions owned by them as well as fire preventative measures or firefighting efforts”, the statement said.

Singapore also said it would form a panel of experts comprising law firms, audit firms and investigative firms with expertise in conducting cross-border inquiries and investigations to help with its probe.

Indonesia experiences fires regularly during its dry season, and experts say years of deforestation and the draining of peatland for cultivation have rendered previously fire-resistant landscapes vulnerable.

Driven by a strong El Nino cycle and resulting drought, this year’s blazes have been particularly severe, burning through nearly two million hectares, according to deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas.
The fires have raged across forests and peatland, as well as palm oil and timber plantations supplying multinational firms.
Civil society groups have regularly accused companies of responsibility for the blazes, pointing to so-called “hotspots” in supplier plantations, sometimes called concessions.

Several companies implicated have insisted they are not behind the fires, including Singapore Exchange-listed First Resources and Singapore-registered Asia Pulp and Paper. Both are named by the NEA in the latest update on Singapore’s probe.
Kuala Lumpur and Singapore again ranked within the world’s top 10 most polluted major cities late Friday, according to Swiss-based air monitor IQAir. — AFP

Previous winners of the sports award include tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal, marathon record-breaker Eliud Kipchoge and US skier Lindsey Vonn.

feb73f849ef2d58e: From Ravinder Singh
While education minister Fadhlina Sidek accurately stated that school caning was still legally allowed, current disciplinary frameworks are clearly falling short.
The regulations meant to ensure a safe and conducive learning environment have not prevented a severe decline in student behaviour, culminating in tragic instances of fatal school violence.
This crisis raises a critical question: have our existing school discipline rules completely failed?
The road to hell begins with good intentions

The Education (School Discipline) Regulations 1959 of Malaysia governs student discipline and corporal punishment in public schools. The red tape that schools must comply with in using the cane makes caning totally useless.

Only the head teacher or a designated teacher can use the cane, not the class teacher; caning must be done privately; another teacher must be present as a witness; details such as the child’s name, offence, punishment, date and time must be recorded.
As the then assistant headmaster of SK Tunku Abdul Halim in Alor Setar, I witnessed a dramatic shift in our school’s trajectory.

It was the premier primary school in northern Kedah during the 1950s and 1960s, but by 1990, when I took charge, it had become one of the worst. Faced with this crisis, I had two choices: allow the decay to continue or use the cane on my own terms to restore order.
I chose to do it my way, even though it bypassed standard disciplinary regulations. The approach worked, and I want to share that experience here.
Mayhem reigned in this school. Unbearable noise, unsightly litter everywhere, teachers screaming at children, children leaving classrooms and loitering, pushing and shoving at the canteen.

I was in total disbelief when the school head said at a staff meeting that “here we practice democracy”. This was clearly directed at me for controlling the “democracy” that children had been given the freedom to practice and pull the school down into the gutter.
Judicious use of the cane worked a miracle

Having given teachers a set of my own “classroom and child management rules” to be strictly implemented, I started my daily two rounds of corridor walking with a cane in hand for on-the-spot shock-giving to the brain to trigger re-wiring of the bad behaviour connections to good.
Of the 600 plus children in this boys’ school, hardly 10% needed the cure. The rest got the clear message that rules had to be obeyed; their previous “democratic” ways were not acceptable to me.
A light cane is most effective during early childhood, that is in pre-school and primary school, which is the critical habit-forming age. Not every child requires it.
However, for those who do, the physical sting serves as a necessary shock, breaking negative behavioural patterns and prompting them to re-evaluate their actions.
It works the same way that cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) does to shock the heart to start functioning again. Like CPR, the cane must be administered immediately after the event, without delay.
The cane was used only on the palms. One parent confronted me as his Year 3 son had a cane mark on his wrist because the boy had pulled his hand away.
“Do you have the authority to cane children?”
“Yes,” I said, as I told him I would not allow his son to disrupt a class of over 30, running around and pulling other children’s books and pencils while they did their work.
He could take his son to another school if he so wished. The son was soon back in school, a changed person. I set the standard, the parents followed.

On the first school day of the new year, I had a dialogue with the parents in the hall. I reminded them of this school’s excellent status in the 1950s and 1960s, and its shameful status now, all because discipline had not been strictly maintained.
To achieve good academic performance, the prerequisite was good discipline. If teachers had to use the cane to restore discipline, it was for the good of the children.
They gave me unanimous support, and I never had an issue with any of them as long as I was there. Teachers were happy they could conduct lessons with children paying attention.

When I left one and a half years later it took just one week for “democracy” to return to the school. It was heartbreaking that no one could continue maintaining the discipline that I had taken so much trouble to restore within three months of taking charge.
False theories surrounding child disciplining issues
There is not a single study of an actual hands-on use of the cane in real-life situations like I did. All other “studies” are based on the results of wrongful use of the cane.
This is like compiling a list of botched medical surgeries and concluding that surgeries can cause deaths and paralysis and therefore should be banned.
In my own way I proved that a light cane, properly used, is an excellent tool for maintaining discipline in primary school. Then, strict discipline has to be maintained in secondary schools.
The education ministry should not dismiss the “grandfathers’ way” of disciplining children. If schools set the discipline standard, parents will respect it and do their part.
When schools accept indiscipline, parents think that is normal and cannot accept when any teacher disciplines their child.
Get it right — every school must set and enforce strict discipline. Only when schools stop accepting indiscipline will parents take the discipline of their children seriously.
Ravinder Singh is an FMT reader.

2bf118ec865eef37: KUALA LUMPUR: It can happen in the middle of the night - an intensely itchy rash suddenly spreads across the body, disturbing sleep and leaving the person wondering what caused it. By the time they reach a clinic, however, the rash may have disappeared.

Dermatologist Dr Peter Ch’ng said this pattern is familiar to people living with chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU). The condition causes recurring itchy, raised hives, sometimes with deeper swelling known as angioedema, for more than six weeks without an obvious external trigger.
“Normally, patients tell me, ‘Doctor, the rash disappeared while I was waiting to see you, but from experience, I’m certain it will come back again’,” he said.

For many patients, the problem extends beyond the skin. Repeated flare-ups and itching can affect sleep, concentration, work and emotional wellbeing, particularly because the next episode is often unpredictable.

Ch’ng said a typical urticaria rash has a smooth, swollen appearance, with individual hives usually disappearing within 24 hours. New ones may then emerge elsewhere, giving the impression that the rash is moving around the body.

Chronic urticaria affects around 1% of people worldwide, although estimates vary. A systematic review of Asian studies found a pooled prevalence of about 1.4%, though this included different forms of chronic urticaria rather than CSU alone.

Some patients mistake the rash for eczema, psoriasis or an allergic reaction. “Getting the diagnosis right matters because similar-looking conditions may require very different management,” Ch’ng said.

He added that haze has not been shown to directly trigger CSU, despite its known effects on conditions such as eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis. Stress, however, may worsen urticaria in some people.
More than ‘just a rash’
A Malaysian study found that more than 80% of patients with CSU reported moderate-to-severe itching and hives, affecting work, social life and daily activities.

Ch’ng recalled treating a young patient whose symptoms were not adequately controlled by antihistamines, the usual first-line treatment. Frequent flare-ups affected his sleep and concentration, and he repeatedly missed classes.
Because hives can fade before a medical appointment, photographs can be particularly useful. Ch’ng advises patients to take clear pictures during a flare and note how the rash behaves.
Useful details include whether it is raised or flat, smooth or rough, whether each flare disappears within 24 hours and whether it leaves bruising or pigmentation behind.

Typical urticaria lesions are usually smooth and transient, disappearing within a day without leaving marks. Rashes that persist, scale, become painful or leave bruise-like changes may point to another condition and should be assessed.
Not every episode of hives is CSU, either. The six-week duration or recurrence threshold is one of the clues doctors use to distinguish chronic disease from a short-lived episode.

Some patients respond to new hives by repeatedly applying steroid cream wherever the rash appears. Ch’ng said this often makes little sense for a condition in which individual lesions vanish quickly and reappear elsewhere.
“Before the steroid cream is absorbed, the rash will likely have appeared on a different part of the body,” he said. “Chasing the rash with steroid cream is not the answer.”
He also cautions against repeated systemic steroid injections as a long-term solution, as they can carry significant health risks.
International guidelines recommend second-generation H1 antihistamines as first-line treatment, with treatment escalated under medical supervision if symptoms remain uncontrolled.

For Ch’ng, the goal is not merely partial improvement. "It is not enough to say the condition has improved by 50% when they still do not know when it will worsen. Clear, symptom-free skin is our target," he said.
b482ac6e1114a80c: Saya petik laporan Berita Harian siaran 22 Okt lalu mengenai ucapan Nik Muhammad Zawawi Salleh, Ahli Parlimen PAS bagi Pasir Putih, yakni ketika beliau membahas Rang Undang-undang Perbekalan 2027 di Parlimen. Beliau gesa kerajaan kurangkan pemberian bantuan tunai dan beri lebih tumpuan kepada usaha memperkasakan rakyat supaya mampu menjana pendapatan sendiri untuk jangka panjang. Ada yang saya setuju, dan ada tidak.

Kata Zawawi, kerajaan perlu mendidik rakyat supaya berusaha mencipta peluang dan bekerja untuk meningkatkan kehidupan. Bagi saya, rakyat tidak perlu diajar oleh kerajaan. Tidak perlu kerajaan berkhutbah menggesa rakyat 'cipta peluang' dan 'kerja' untuk tingkatkan tahap kehidupan, sebab sememangnya rakyat terutama golongan miskin tahu itu semua. Mereka tahu apa yang perlu dilakukan untuk survive dan tingkatkan kehidupan.
That's what they have been doing all this while.

Sememangnya rakyat sentiasa bekerja (dengan keras) serta mencari dan mengintai peluang untuk senang dan menikmati lebih kesenangan. They don’t need the government to lecture or teach what they have to do to improve their livelihood.

Berkata lagi Zawawi: "kalau kita ada peruntukan, rakyat kita bagi 'kail', jangan kita bagi 'ikan'". Umum faham yang dimaksudkan beliau. Benar ada pepatah Inggeris, "give a man a fish and you feed him for a day, teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime".

Comedian terkenal, Trevor Noah, menambah "and it would be nice if you gave him a fishing rod". Zawawi got it right on this. Berikan 'kail' kepada rakyat bagi membolehkan mereka mendapat 'ikan' buat selama-lamanya.

Namun dalam menyatakan beri rakyat 'kail', Zawawi juga berkata, "kalau kita bagi subsidi, kita bagi 'ikan', dia mengajar rakyat ini malas". Maksudnya beliau menyamakan pemberian subsidi dengan pemberian 'ikan', dan buat rakyat malas. Ini pelik dan saya tidak setuju.

Bagaimana 'subsidi' boleh dikaitkan dengan 'malas'? Subsidi ke atas barangan keperluan misalnya ialah bagi meringankan beban rakyat untuk memiliki barangan berkenaan, membolehkan rakyat mampu beli apa yang mereka perlu. Rakyat masih perlu bekerja untuk mendapat duit untuk membeli barangan yang disubsidi. Kata kuncinya 'beli', bukan percuma.

Walaupun barang dibeli pada harga lebih rendah daripada harga asal tanpa subsidi, tetapi hakikatnya kena beli. Untuk beli perlu duit. Untuk dapat duit, rakyat perlu bekerja. Jadi apabila rakyat bekerja, mereka bukan malas. Maka tidak adil dan tidak betul untuk kata subsidi buat rakyat malas. Jika ada pihak yang risau mengenai subsidi, it's the government kerana subsidi boleh membebankan.

Seterusnya Zawawi dipetik berkata: "kalau kita bagi duit, kalau dia boleh guna seminggu, seminggu habis". Money is meant to be spent. Kalau duit digunakan untuk beli barangan keperluan atau perbelanjaan penting seperti tambang anak ke sekolah dan buku tambahan maka tidak ada dosanya duit habis dalam seminggu. Mereka bukan joli sehingga duit habis.

Zawawi juga berkata: "tapi kalau kita bagi periuk, kuali, kita bagi mesin, kita bagi alat, dia boleh gunakan alat ini bertahun-tahun dan mungkin dia boleh bangkit dengan baik". Betul kata-kata itu. Bagaimanapun apa yang boleh dilakukan dengan kuali, periuk, mesin tanpa bahan memasak misalnya?

Bagaimana mahu perolehi bahan-bahan itu? Pastinya terpaksa dibeli. Macam mana mahu beli? Perlu duit. Ertinya bantuan duit tetap diperlukan untuk beri si penerima kuali, periuk dan mesin a head start. Perlu diingat juga keluar rumah untuk pergi kerja pun memerlukan duit. Nothing is free, my friend, apa lagi pada zaman ini.

Untuk berlaku adil, perlu dinyatakan Zawawi tidak menafikan terdapat golongan memerlukan bantuan kewangan termasuk ibu tunggal, yang mempunyai ramai anak dan sukar bekerja selain golongan sakit serta orang kurang upaya. This is stating the obvious.
Artikel ini ialah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
75bd2751cb132f4c: WASHINGTON: The US Defence Department has designated Chinese-funded cultural centres on university campuses known as Confucius Institutes as a threat to US national security, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said on Friday.
Washington has long accused Confucius Institutes of being Chinese propaganda tools and has taken steps to crack down on them.

Hegseth, in a video posted on social media, alleged that Confucius Institutes were operating under disguise at US universities and that the Pentagon had added them to its list of institutions that threaten US national security.

"It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: To steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students," Hegseth said.
The Defence Department had "systematically dismantled every single one of these organisations" over the past two months, he said.
The Chinese embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
0dbef00396bd9bca: GENEVA: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said.
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.

"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work," he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial "shortly", CEPI said in a statement.

"Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks," said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
'Important step'
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.

"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus -- a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives," he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
"Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities," said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO two days later triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.
e24182b669974eb9: KUALA LUMPUR: Goh Sze Fei-Nur Izzuddin produced one of their finest performances of the season to send world No. 1 Kim Won Ho-Seo Seung Jae crashing out of the French Open on Friday, keeping alive hopes of an all-Malaysian men's doubles final.
The world No. 5 took 36 minutes to overcome the top-seeded South Koreans 21-15, 21-18 at Arena Grand Paris, earning their place in the semi-finals of the Super 750 tournament.
It was a remarkable victory for the sixth seeds, who had lost their previous two encounters against the Koreans at the Japan Open and World Championships in August.
Sze Fei-Izzuddin have now beaten Won Ho-Seung Jae three times in seven meetings, including their Indonesia Open semi-final victory in June.
Sze Fei admitted that they were surprised by the Koreans' approach but credited their own ability to make the most of their physical condition.
"I don't know what happened to them. Maybe they tried to change their style, but we just tried to enjoy the game," said Sze Fei in a post-match interview with the Badminton World Federation.
"To be honest, we're not 100 per cent fit, so we tried to focus more on the quality of our strokes. That worked well."
Izzuddin said communication and discipline were equally important in overcoming the Koreans.
"The key was to enjoy our match, communicate with each other and stick with the game plan," he said.

It was also the second consecutive week that Kim Won Ho-Seo Seung Jae, who appeared almost invincible last season, had fallen to a Malaysian pair, following their defeat to Aaron Chia-Soh Wooi Yik in the Denmark Open semi-finals.
Sze Fei-Izzuddin will next face Indonesia's world No. 25 Leo Rolly Carnando-Daniel Marthin, against whom they hold a 2-0 head-to-head advantage.

A victory on Saturday would send them into their fourth World Tour final of the season, having already captured the Indonesia Masters and Indonesia Open titles while finishing runners-up at the Malaysia Masters.
Malaysia could even have two pairs contesting in Sunday's final, with Man Wei Chong-Tee Kai Wun also reaching the semi-finals, although under unfortunate circumstances.
The world No. 11 were leading Aaron-Wooi Yik 5-0 in the opening game when their senior compatriots retired after just two minutes.
The reason for the fourth seeds' retirement was not immediately known.

Ironically, it was a reversal of fortunes from the World Championships in August, when Wei Chong-Kai Wun handed Aaron-Wooi Yik a walkover in their all-Malaysian last-16 encounter after Kai Wun fell ill.
This time, it was Wei Chong-Kai Wun who benefited from their compatriots' misfortune.
They will next face Indonesia's world No. 14 Raymond Indra-Nikolaus Joaquin, who won their only previous meeting.
Victories for both Malaysian pairs would set up an all-Malaysian final in Paris, adding another memorable chapter to the country's strong showing in men's doubles in the European swing.
