dcca69281910f762: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 24 — While haze exposure poses health risks to the general population, high-risk groups such as children, older adults and pregnant women are more vulnerable to its effects.

However, medical and health experts say no single group among those considered high-risk is necessarily more vulnerable than others, with susceptibility depending on factors such as age, underlying medical conditions and the duration and intensity of exposure.
Those with chronic lung diseases and other medical conditions are also among those who need to take precautions against haze exposure.
How haze affects high-risk groups

Universiti Malaya Faculty of Medicine’s social and preventive medicine department public health medicine specialist Dr Bala Murali Sundram said there was no single group among those considered high-risk that was more vulnerable than others.
He told Malay Mail that young children with asthma, older adults with heart or lung diseases, and pregnant women with underlying medical conditions may be especially susceptible during haze episodes.

Dr Bala, who is also the department’s Occupational and Environmental Health senior medical lecturer, said the risks vary according to age, existing medical conditions, and the duration and intensity of exposure.

“Children, especially those below five years of age, are more susceptible because their lungs and immune systems are still developing. They also breathe more air relative to their body weight and may spend more time being physically active.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
File picture of a mother helping her child put on a face mask. — Picture by Sayuti Zainudin

“Older adults, defined in Malaysia as individuals aged 60 years and above, face increased risks because of age-related physiological changes and the higher prevalence of chronic disease,” he said, adding that haze can aggravate asthma, respiratory and cardiovascular conditions, potentially increasing the risk of hospitalisation, heart attacks and even strokes.
Pregnant women are another high-risk group, with Dr Bala saying epidemiological evidence links exposure to air pollution during pregnancy to adverse birth outcomes.
He said these include preterm birth and low birth weight.
“However, the risk depends on the timing, intensity and duration of exposure, and a brief haze episode does not necessarily result in pregnancy complications,” he noted.
Respiratory conditions and other health risks

Pantai Hospital Batu Pahat consultant internal medicine specialist, gastroenterologist and hepatologist Dr Mohamed Amin Kader said there was usually no single test to confirm an illness caused by haze exposure.
He told Malay Mail that diagnosis was based on symptoms, exposure, the patient’s medical history, underlying health conditions and clinical findings.
General practitioner Dr Boo Cheng Hau said most haze-related cases, particularly among high-risk groups, involved respiratory problems.
The former Johor assemblyman said these included acute exacerbations of bronchial asthma among children and adults, as well as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease among older adults.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A woman wears a face mask as she walks along a street in Kuala Lumpur on October 19, 2026. — AFP pic
“In addition, there is the issue of related allergic reactions and nasal congestion due to allergic rhinitis,” he said when contacted by Malay Mail.
Dr Boo said children could face more serious long-term effects because they would be breathing toxic gases and polluted air over a much longer period if the haze problem persisted.
Medical specialist Dr Norafiza Mohd Yasin said children with bronchial asthma, chronic respiratory illnesses or primary immunodeficiency may face a higher risk of complications.
She told Malay Mail that those undergoing chemotherapy or recovering from it may also be more vulnerable if their immune systems were suppressed.
What in haze can affect your health?
Dr Norafiza highlighted the risks associated with exposure to fine particulate matter known as PM2.5.

“The PM2.5 particles can penetrate deep into the lungs and may enter the bloodstream, worsening respiratory and cardiovascular conditions,” she cautioned, adding that pregnant women should also take precautions, as exposure to PM2.5 has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including preterm birth and low birth weight.
Dr Mohamed Amin said PM2.5 particles could penetrate deep into the lungs and contribute to lung infections and pneumonia among high-risk groups.
He said children, particularly those below two years old, were more vulnerable.
“As their lung capacities are not fully developed yet, the haze can also aggravate asthma and trigger worsening respiratory symptoms,” he said.

The World Health Organisation defines PM2.5 as a mixture of solid and liquid particles, with major components including sulphates, nitrates, ammonia, sodium chloride, black carbon, mineral dust and water.
It also notes that PM2.5 can originate from direct emissions as well as chemical reactions between gases in the atmosphere.
Taking the right precautions
With air quality reaching unhealthy levels, health and medical experts advise the public to take steps to reduce their exposure to haze.
These include:
Wearing an N95 respirator when going outdoors to reduce exposure.
Staying indoors as much as possible, limiting unnecessary outdoor activities and prolonged exposure.
Taking extra precautions to protect children, older adults, pregnant women and people with respiratory or heart conditions.
Monitoring air quality in their respective areas.
fd9bcd7de19956c0: TOKYO, Oct 24 — At a barbershop in Tokyo, yakuza gangster Tekisasu glances in the mirror at his meticulous new cut and thanks the hairdresser for the weekly trim crucial to his mobster trade.
Japan’s yakuza operate an organised crime empire worth billions of dollars and have long dominated the country’s drug rings, gambling dens and sex trade.
From precise haircuts to sharp suits, many mobsters try to project an image of menace and wealth, and barbers play a key role in crafting it.
“The yakuza are all about vanity,” said Tekisasu, whose moniker means “Enemy Stabber”, in an exclusive interview that took months to set up.
“The neater someone’s appearance, the better his reputation becomes,” the 44-year-old active gangster allied to a major clan told AFP.
“Say you want to sell someone on a deal... they won’t take you seriously if your punch perm is all in shambles,” he said, referencing his ultra-short, tightly curled style.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 27, 2026 shows Tekisasu, an active yakuza gangster allied to a major clan, having his hair permed at a barbershop in Tokyo. — AFP pic
For Tekisasu and his fellow mobsters, barbershops also represent a break from the violent lifestyle they have chosen and an intensifying crackdown by authorities.
During his monthly, two-hour perming ritual — plus a weekly haircut that keeps the back and sides of his head shaven in a high “skin fade” — the tattooed gangster can stop watching his back.
There are fewer and fewer mobsters like him, with police saying yakuza numbers dipped last year to a record low of 17,600 nationwide.
But even as their forces shrink, the gangsters represent a potent threat, with younger groups of thugs brought in to diversify their business, police warned in a recent report.

Still, Tekisasu’s barber — who counts around 10 active yakuza among his repeat clientele — says he has no qualms about serving them, even though his craftsmanship amplifies their “don’t-mess-with-me aura”.
“All I do is make them look cooler,” said the 32-year-old, denying there was anything wrong in making dangerous gangsters appear more aggressive.
The barber requested anonymity because any association with the mafia could threaten the reputation of his business.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 27, 2026 shows Tekisasu, an active yakuza gangster allied to a major clan, having his beard trimmed at a barbershop in Tokyo. — AFP pic
Grinding out a living
Despite their criminal activities, many people — including some of the gangsters themselves — hold romantic views of the yakuza’s traditions, lifestyles and codes of honour.
The reality is often more mundane, with more and more rank-and-file mobsters said to grind out a living by targeting vulnerable people through crimes such as organised fraud.
Originally a gangsta rapper, Tekisasu delved into the yakuza world in his mid-20s, but was arrested in 2021, then jailed, before being released last year.
Now, he is at the barbershop for a hot-towel shave and respite from a life where he says, “total darkness can be just an inch ahead”.
“When there is fighting among syndicates, we have no choice but to go through it,” he said. “It’s a matter of pride.”
“I wish I could just live smiling, without hurting anyone or getting hurt. But that’s not how things work in this world.”
Yakuza face pressure to remain in the violent underworld, but they can and do choose to leave. An estimated 320 gangsters quit in 2024 thanks in part to efforts by authorities.
Under Tokyo’s anti-yakuza laws, businesses are prohibited from knowingly “providing benefits” to mobsters to aid their activities.
Barbers who intentionally help yakuza clients maintain their looks are unlikely to violate the rules, provided the transactions are fair, according to retired anti-mafia detective Yuichi Sakurai.
But any preferential treatment, like “setting the haircut price excessively low”, may constitute an illegal favour, he told AFP.
In his decades-long career, the ex-detective himself noticed many mobsters “value frequent haircuts to retain their intimidating exteriors”.
Ideally, the laws should be tightened to bar the yakuza from any place of relaxation — including barbershops — “if we really want to eradicate them”, he said.
Years of strict anti-mafia laws have excluded the yakuza from basic infrastructure in Japan, including opening bank accounts, renting housing and obtaining credit cards.
“We can only pay in cash most of the time. It would be very tough for us if Japan ever fully goes cashless,” Tekisasu said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photo taken on August 27, 2026 shows Tekisasu, an active yakuza gangster allied to a major clan, showing his tattoos on his leg at a barbershop in Tokyo. — AFP pic
‘Rival gangsters’
Far from being dismayed that gangsters frequent his parlour, Tekisasu’s barber is proud that they trust his “uncompromising standards”.
Following in the footsteps of his barber father, adept at a range of “bad-boy” haircuts, he has made punch perms his forte.
The tiny, rigid curls emerged in Japan in the 1960s and ‘70s as a backlash against longer, Beatles-inspired male hairdos.
They have since found a devoted fanbase in manual labourers, teen delinquents and the yakuza.
“Punch perms are what I live for as a barber,” said the gregarious shopkeeper, whose full-arm tattoos include depictions of scissors, a comb and a dryer.
When a client who was “obviously yakuza, with his fingertip missing and eyes dead serious”, first sought his service, he resolved to “blow him away with my skills” and make him a regular.
While lore has it that yakuza gangsters found the punch perm’s ultra-short length useful during brawls, Tekisasu says that in his world, “fights don’t usually involve hair-pulling”.
“When we ‘fight,’ it’s ultimately about shooting or trying to take each other’s lives,” he said.
“I simply like the punch perm because it’s manly and cool.”
Yakuza patronage involves risks, however.
“The last thing I want is for rival gangsters to run into each other here,” Tekisasu’s barber said. The onus is thus on him to space their appointments apart.
But “once they leave the shop, whatever happens out there is going to happen. When they walk out the door, I don’t talk to them anymore.” — AFP
ad458422992cbe30: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 24 — Haze pushed air quality to hazardous levels in parts of the country this year, with the Air Pollutant Index (API) peaking at 519 in six areas of Sarawak on September 1.

Readings above 300 are classified as hazardous, while those recorded across parts of Peninsular Malaysia in October, including Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, Negeri Sembilan and Johor, mostly ranged from 101 to 210, within the unhealthy category.
While haze is commonly associated with respiratory and cardiovascular problems, medical experts say it can also affect the skin and eyes.
How haze affects skin and eyes

Medical specialist Dr Norafiza Mohd Yasin said PM2.5 particles, which measure 2.5 microns in diameter, can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, as well as disrupt the skin’s natural barrier.
“When PM2.5 particles infiltrate the pores, they disrupt the skin’s natural barrier.
“This leads to increased sensitivity, dryness, and irritation, often triggering flare-ups of underlying conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, and acne,” she said when contacted by Malay Mail.

Dr Bala Murali Sundram, a public health medicine specialist at Universiti Malaya’s Faculty of Medicine, said pollutants deposited on exposed skin can contribute to oxidative stress, inflammation and damage to the skin barrier.
“This may cause itching, dryness and redness or aggravate existing conditions such as eczema and atopic dermatitis,” he explained.

Pantai Hospital Batu Pahat consultant internal medicine specialist, gastroenterologist and hepatologist Dr Mohamed Amin Kader said fine particles in haze can cause dry eyes, redness and a stinging sensation.
“This ultimately can cause eye infection such as conjunctivitis if left untreated,” he said when contacted by Malay Mail.

Dr Bala, who is also a senior medical lecturer in the department’s Occupational and Environmental Health unit, said airborne pollutants can disturb the tear film and irritate the surface of the eyes, causing redness, burning, stinging, watery eyes and dryness.
“Individuals with dry-eye disease, allergies or contact lens use may experience greater discomfort,” he said.
How to reduce exposure
Dr Norafiza advised people to reduce unnecessary outdoor activities, particularly when the API reaches unhealthy levels.
“Staying indoors and keeping indoor air clean are important preventive measures.

“When outdoor exposure is unavoidable, a properly fitted N95 respirator can help reduce the inhalation of fine particles, although it does not protect against gaseous pollutants,” she said, adding that respirator suitability should be considered carefully for children, pregnant women and people with underlying medical conditions.
She advised the public to seek medical attention if symptoms persist or worsen, particularly in cases of eye pain, blurred vision, breathing difficulty or worsening asthma symptoms.

“Ultimately, prevention is key. Monitoring air quality, reducing unnecessary outdoor exposure and taking appropriate precautions are essential to protecting vulnerable groups during haze episodes,” she said.
Dr Bala advised the public to minimise unnecessary outdoor exposure, particularly when the API exceeds 100, and to avoid rubbing irritated eyes.
Contact lens users exposed to irritating dust or particles should remove their lenses before rinsing their eyes with clean water or sterile saline, he said.
Dr Bala also advised against using harsh soaps, vigorous scrubbing and excessive washing, which may worsen skin irritation.
He recommended keeping windows closed during heavy haze and using suitable air filtration at home where available to maintain cleaner indoor air.
7c5c8f109c7713a7: NAPA (California), Oct 24 — Napa Valley rocketed to international fame when its vintages shocked French rivals in a high-profile blind tasting contest that instantly turned the California corner into a wine-lovers’ destination.
Now, Donald Trump’s unpredictable tariff policies and attacks on traditional allies are souring the area’s relationship with the foreign tourists and international markets it has grown to depend on.

“Napa Valley is proudly one of the most global, if not the most global destination in the United States for wine,” Linsey Gallagher, president of Visit Napa Valley, an organisation representing the region’s hotel industry, told AFP.
“But at the moment that piece of the business is a little bit challenged.”

Napa announced itself to the global wine-drinking public in dramatic fashion in 1976, when two of its vintages, a red and a white, won the Judgment of Paris, a blind tasting judged by nine experts, most of them French.

“Napa did not have any publicity, and then all of a sudden, the few journalists wrote articles, and Napa became a buzzing place,” said Ivo Jeramaz, whose uncle, Mike Grgich, made the 1973 Chateau Montelena Chardonnay that was named best white at the competition.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This aerial view shows tourists visiting the Castello di Amorosa winery in Calistoga, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
“The wealthy clients started coming, money started pouring in.”
The region boomed, said Jeramaz, who now runs Grgich Hills Estate, and spends hours talking with visitors who come to taste his wines.
But the excitement of the last few decades has cooled, he said, a situation exacerbated by tariffs that the US president has imposed on countries that buy California wine.
“Nobody is benefiting from tariffs,” said Jeramaz, who blames them for raising production costs and hurting exports.
“We were selling over 1,000 cases, which is for us a good amount of wine, to Canada, and now we have zero since tariffs. So it’s a big problem.”
Ottawa and Washington are locked in a deep trade dispute, exacerbated by Trump’s frequent insults and claims that Canada will be taken over as a 51st US state.
In response, some Canadian provinces have pulled US goods from their shelves and tourists who would otherwise have headed south have voted with their feet and stayed home.
“It’s a big, big hit,” said Jeramaz.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
A tourist takes a chance to try the wine grape-stomping process at Grgich Hills Estate in Rutherford, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
International component

About 20 per cent of visitors to the region used to come from abroad, drawn by a Mediterranean-style climate, tranquil vineyards and lively towns full of restaurants and fashionable shops. That share has fallen to eight per cent.
“The biggest impact for us comes from the decline in Canadian visitors,” said Gallagher.
In an effort to fill the gap, businesses have focused their advertising efforts on the domestic market.
The strategy appears to be working for now.
Last year the valley welcomed around 3.8 million people, up three per cent from pre-pandemic tourism levels.
“But we’re only going to be able to extract so much out of that domestic and local market. We won’t fully recover until that international piece comes back,” Gallagher warned.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Wine grapes are processed on a conveyor belt at Grgich Hills Estate in Rutherford, in California’s Napa Valley October 5, 2026. — AFP pic
Wellness, Napa-style
Changing consumption habits among younger generations are also weighing on Napa Valley, where more than 1,000 vineyards line a nearly 37-mile (60-kilometre) stretch traversed by a tourist train.
Winemakers are trying to understand and adapt to these new customers who care more about environmental and social justice practices than about brands.

“When we get our wines in front of younger consumers and tell them the story of how they’re made, how the grapes are grown, that it is a living, breathing, beautiful agricultural product, they’re excited to discover something new,” said Ali van Zyl, owner of the Belong Wine Company label.
Another way to draw visitors is to highlight the valley’s natural attractions and its food and hotel offerings.
Tourism managers hope it could reposition Napa as a destination for people seeking a healthy lifestyle.
“Sharing a bottle of wine is a lot different than taking a bunch of tequila shots,” said Laura Gabriel, van Zyl’s partner in the River Club tasting house.
“It is a natural product and it’s a part of well-lived life, with hiking and being outdoors and cooking,” said Gabriel. “That’s the Napa form of wellness.” — AFP
0151d02ea7e7d46c: LONDON, Oct 24 — Ahead of next month’s midterm US elections, Donald Trump has increasingly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging energy prices back home, which are causing the president political headaches.
However, analysts say the main driver of higher fuel prices remains the US-Iran war.
Which Russian sites have been targeted?
Ukraine has intensified its drone attacks on Russia’s energy industry over the past 18 months, seeking to cut the Kremlin’s revenues and undermine its ability to finance the war.
The strikes have targeted “mostly refineries”, Julien Mathonniere, an economist at Energy Intelligence, told AFP.
On average, one Russian refinery was hit every three days during the first eight months of the year, according to the International Energy Agency.

“Russia’s net diesel exports fell by approximately 80 per cent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, from around 1.05 million barrels per day to just 200,000 barrels per day,” said Viktor Kurilov, an analyst at Rystad Energy.
In response to the disruption in domestic fuel supplies, Moscow introduced a ban on diesel exports from July until the end of October.
Why does this concern Trump?
Trump has repeatedly condemned the attacks on Russian refineries, saying Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky disobeyed his orders to halt the strikes.
By contrast, Trump has not commented on the intensification in recent months of Russian strikes against Ukrainian territory, which have caused a surge in civilian casualties.
Trump’s frustrations come as the Republicans face dim prospects in the November midterm elections, partly because of soaring fuel prices.
US diesel prices at the pump climbed to a record of US$6.53 (RM26.67) per gallon at the end of September, up from US$3.75 per gallon before the war, according to the American Automobile Association.
Energy price rises are also fuelling inflation across the economy.
What is the Mideast role?
Ukraine’s strikes explain “about one-third of the global diesel shortfall, currently estimated at 1.7 to 1.8 million barrels per day”, said Mathonniere.

But “the impact of previous drone strikes (by Kyiv) on global product prices before the Middle East crisis was minimal”, James Henderson, a researcher at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, told AFP.
Energy exports from the Gulf have plunged since US-Israeli strikes on Iran from February caused Tehran to respond by choking off the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas transit.
At the same time, maritime freight costs have soared and major refining capacity in the Middle East has been hit, adding to upward pressure on oil prices.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Relations between Kyiv and Washington soured further this month after Trump announced a controversial agreement with Moscow to lift certain sanctions and allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices. — Picture by Raymond Manuel
Can prices fall before midterms?

Relations between Kyiv and Washington soured further this month after Trump announced a controversial agreement with Moscow to lift certain sanctions and allow Russian diesel imports, supposedly to ease prices.

The US president said Wednesday that he believed an end to the Russia-Ukraine war could be closer than ever, as the Kremlin said it was willing to restart trilateral talks with Kyiv and Washington next month.
For now, however, the strikes continue.
“There’s not much that can be done in the very short term to lower diesel prices,” said Jorge Leon, an analyst at Rystad Energy.
Even if the Russia conflict ended or an energy ceasefire was reached, the impact “wouldn’t really move the needle massively for the US midterm elections”, he added.
Repairs to damaged infrastructure take time, while continued hostilities in the Middle East drive energy prices higher. — AFP
9ae6c926dda75aa0: NEW DELHI, Oct 24 — Fiercely proud of its culinary traditions, India is increasingly open to foreign influences, with French cooking schools attracting students eager to make their mark on the country’s growing fine-dining sector.

“Ten or 15 years ago, there were far fewer young people dreaming of becoming chefs,” said Aabhas Jain, director of bakery and pastry training at Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school also operating in India.

“But with the rise of social media... today’s students have greater ambitions in this profession,” added Jain, 36, who is also part of the Indian School of Hospitality (ISH) in Gurugram, just outside New Delhi.

In the world’s most populous country, the need for high-end hospitality workers is immense, fuelled by economic growth and the rise of a middle class that travels more and increasingly eats at plush establishments.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 22, 2026 shows head of Vatel Hotel and Tourism Business School Saurav Chhabra speaking during an interview with AFP in Gurugram. — AFP pic
“There are plenty of job opportunities,” said Saurav Chhabra, head of French hotel school Vatel’s Indian campus, which has been based in Gurugram since 2015 in partnership with Sushant University.
“Employers’ expectations are very high, particularly in five-star hotel chains.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 22, 2026 shows a student chef preparing the classic French dish ‘Poulet sauté chasseur’ at the Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school in Gurugram. — AFP pic
‘Braising, blanching’
Culinary and pastry courses, once relatively rare in India, have proliferated over the past decade, with foreign private schools helping drive its high-end hospitality sector.
Such is the enthusiasm that France is considering opening vocational schools, notably in Puducherry, the former French colonial port in India’s southeast.
Ecole Ducasse has more than 600 students, most from affluent backgrounds.

Indian chefs who have worked at prestigious restaurants, including overseas, teach their respective specialties: Indian, European, Mediterranean and Asian cuisine, as well as bakery and pastry-making.
Siddhant Marwah, a final-year student, joined the school to acquire “French techniques that represent the quintessence of culinary expertise.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 22, 2026 shows French dishes prepared by student chefs at the Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school in Gurugram. — AFP

As he puts the finishing touches to a gratin dauphinois — a dish of sliced potatoes baked in cream — he explains that French and Indian cuisines share techniques such as “braising, blanching, and slow cooking in stews.”
While France boasts its beef bourguignon, India is not to be outdone with goat nihari, a meat dish cooked for hours in a spicy broth.
Drawn by the opportunities for travel and meeting people that a career as a chef offers, Marwah already dreams of opening his own restaurant in India.
Nearby, Amitabh Sukhwal has just enrolled at Vatel, whose tuition fees are considerably lower than those at Ecole Ducasse.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 22, 2026 shows a staff member putting a badge on a mannequin during a class at the Vatel Hotel and Tourism Business School in Gurugram. — AFP pic
The school has around 120 students, many from modest backgrounds.

Sukhwal, 18, who calls himself a “lover of the French language”, plans to go to France in four years to pursue a master’s degree, gain experience abroad and then draw on it to open his own hotel in India.

He learned French through interactions with guests at the small hotel run by his parents in Chittorgarh, Rajasthan and is now honing his skills at his new school, where French-language classes are compulsory.
‘In vogue’
A majority of the students interviewed by AFP at the two schools plan to remain in India.
After working for many years in India’s luxury hotels, chef Shikha Gupta, who teaches bakery and pastry-making at Vatel, is pleased to see her classes have “as many men as women.”
“Over the past 10 to 12 years, attitudes have changed and many women have chosen to enter the culinary profession,” said Ecole Ducasse’s Aabhas Jain.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This photograph taken on September 22, 2026 shows student chefs working in a kitchen at the Ecole Ducasse, a French culinary school in Gurugram. — AFP pic
“We now see near parity, or even a ratio of 60 per cent women to 40 per cent men.”
Anusha Nagia, who joined Ecole Ducasse in 2024, hopes to open a restaurant in India and one day earn a Michelin star, perhaps by betting on fusion cuisine, which is “very much in vogue.”

While chicken chasseur is one of her favourite French dishes, she fondly recalls a galantine — a French preparation of stuffed meat — in which she and her classmates incorporated the spicy flavours of chicken tikka. — AFP
ab090f4b4e5f1f6c: During his recent visit to Washington, Chinese president Xi Jinping announced that China would send a breeding pair of giant pandas to Zoo Atlanta. The “envoys of friendship,” Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, arrived just a few days later.

This is hardly the first time China has used its iconic bear as an instrument of soft power. By loaning the animals to overseas zoos, it seeks to project an image of China not as a threatening dragon, but rather as a tough but cuddly charmer.

But perhaps the true message of this “panda diplomacy” lies in the manipulation and exploitation it embodies. For starters, while China claims the familiar black-and-white bear as its mascot, one of the species’ primary natural habitats is Wolong, which sits on the steep edge of the Tibetan Plateau.

Within a horizontal distance of about 30 miles, elevations range from alpine peaks exceeding 17,000 feet to below 1,600 feet, creating a moist, temperate microclimate that sustains the high-altitude bamboo forests where pandas thrive.

Historically part of the Tibetan region of Kham, Wolong is now under Sichuan provincial jurisdiction, in Aba Tibetan-Qiang Autonomous Prefecture—and China is all too eager to subsume everything that makes it culturally unique.

Since China’s annexation of resource-rich Tibet in 1950-51, the government has systematically sought to erase Tibetan culture and identity, not least by incorporating the Plateau’s distinctive geography, wildlife, and natural resources into mainstream Chinese national identity.
China’s appropriation of others extends even to cherry-tree cultivation, which it has claimed began not in Japan or Korea, but in “China’s Himalayan highlands”—that is, Tibet.
The Tibetan Plateau is home to the endangered red panda, a house-cat-sized mammal with a long, bushy tail, in addition to giant pandas, which are classified as a vulnerable species.

There are fewer than 2,000 giant pandas left in the wild, and China claims ownership of almost all of them. This brings us to the second dubious element of China’s panda diplomacy: it is based on a lucrative “rent-a-panda-pair” programme.

While China reaps the soft-power benefits of keeping its endearing mascot in foreign zoos, it also charges those zoos high prices: up to US$1.1 million per year for the right to display and breed a pair of pandas. China retains ownership not only of the leased adults, but also of any offspring they produce.

And yet, the leasing zoo must pay a one-time fee of approximately US$600,000 for each cub that is born during its lease. Facilities also often pay up to US$2 million in additional sponsorship and research commitments.

The bills add up. Between 1994 and 2023, China raked in almost US$300 million from its panda-rental programme. Small wonder the Guinness World Records lists the giant panda as the “most expensive species in captivity”.

But the money is just the start. The increasingly one-sided contracts that the state-run China Wildlife Conservation Association signs with zoos allow China to unilaterally terminate an agreement and prematurely recall pandas for various reasons, such as the “unauthorised release of relevant information” to the public.

This includes information that is seemingly innocuous: China prohibits zoos from using terms such as “lease,” “rental,” “loan,” or “contract,” apparently to obscure the transactional nature of the arrangement.
China also uses panda loans to send political messages. China gave a pair of pandas to the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in 1972, following President Richard Nixon’s visit to Beijing.
In 2010, however, it accelerated the recall of two US-born panda cubs after the White House announced that President Barack Obama would not cancel a meeting with the Dalai Lama.
In 2023, the three remaining pandas at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo were returned to China, marking the end of a tradition that had lasted more than a half-century.
And it is not just the US. This year, Japan returned its last two giant pandas to China, leaving it without any for the first time since normalising relations with China in 1972.
By contrast, when China sent a pair of pandas to Qatar before the 2022 World Cup, officials hailed the move as a reflection of the countries’ “depth of relations”.

But the power of China’s panda diplomacy now seems to be waning. While the general public might still find pandas appealing, visits to panda-hosting zoos tend to plateau after the novelty wears off. Meanwhile, conservationists loudly criticise the commercial and diplomatic use of a vulnerable species.

Most importantly for China, political analysts and lawmakers increasingly view panda loans as more of a charming distraction than a meaningful barometer of bilateral relations. This helps to explain why Xi’s recent “gift” to Zoo Atlanta attracted little US media coverage.
With active international panda-leasing programmes having dropped from 21 countries in 2019 to just 16 today, even Chinese state media are now asking whether panda diplomacy has “lost its sparkle”.

Giant pandas may appear cuddly and docile, but they are formidable bears with long, sharp claws and a highly developed jaw structure, which delivers a bite force of nearly 1,300 Newtons, almost on par with that of lions.

While captive-bred pandas introduced into the wild tend to die because they lack critical survival skills, wild pandas can be aggressive and dangerous. In this sense, perhaps pandas really are an accurate symbol of China: even when it appears harmless, it cannot conceal its teeth.
Brahma Chellaney is professor emeritus of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research and a fellow at the Robert Bosch Academy in Berlin.

93748fb9421f2e1b: Jumlah kehadiran Presiden PAS Hadi Awang ke sidang Dewan Rakyat sering menjadi polemik, terutama apabila lawan politik menggunakannya untuk mempersoalkan tanggungjawab beliau sebagai Ahli Parlimen Marang.

Justeru, apabila Hadi hadir ke Dewan, kelibatnya hampir pasti mendapat perhatian. Begitulah keadaannya pada 12 Okt lalu apabila beliau duduk sebaris dengan Ketua Pembangkang Hamzah Zainudin ketika presiden Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan) itu mengambil giliran membahaskan Belanjawan 2027.
Selepas Hamzah selesai berucap, kedua-duanya turut bersama sebahagian besar Ahli Parlimen pembangkang yang hadir.
Pada zahirnya, kedua-dua momen itu mungkin tidak membawa apa-apa makna luar biasa. Seorang presiden parti hadir mendengar ketua pembangkang berbahas, kemudian bergambar bersama rakan-rakan politik.
Namun, dalam landskap politik semasa, apatah lagi ketika PRU16 semakin menghampiri, perkara yang kelihatan biasa kadangkala mengundang tafsiran lebih luas.

Satu persoalan yang mungkin timbul ialah sama ada kehadiran Hadi sekadar tanda sokongan kepada Hamzah sebagai ketua pembangkang, atau mencerminkan keyakinan lebih besar terhadap pemimpin berkenaan dalam percaturan selepas PRU16.

Persoalan itu menjadi relevan apabila parti-parti pembangkang kini mencari bentuk kerjasama baharu selepas pembatalan pendaftaran Perikatan Nasional (PN), dengan PAS, Wawasan, Gerakan, Pejuang dan MIPP antara parti berpotensi bergerak dalam satu jajaran politik.
(Mahkamah Tinggi Kuala Lumpur pada 22 Okt membenarkan permohonan PN untuk menangguhkan pelaksanaan keputusan Jabatan Pendaftaran Pertubuhan Malaysia yang membatalkan pendaftaran gabungan itu.)

Nama Menteri Besar Terengganu Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar tentunya tidak boleh diketepikan. Naib presiden PAS itu sudah lama disebut sebagai antara pemimpin berpotensi diketengahkan ke peringkat nasional, malah pernah dilantik ketua pembangkang ketika PN masih berfungsi sebagai sebuah gabungan.
Namun, perkembangan selepas itu memberi satu dimensi lain.

Jun lalu, Hadi mengumumkan Hamzah akan kembali menjadi ketua pembangkang selepas Samsuri memegang jawatan itu untuk tempoh singkat. Keputusan berkenaan dibuat selepas sokongan majoriti Ahli Parlimen pembangkang beralih semula kepada Hamzah.
Ia bukan kali pertama Hamzah mendapat kepercayaan politik yang mempunyai kaitan dengan PAS.
Selepas PRU15, pelantikannya sebagai ketua pembangkang juga dibuat susulan cadangan PAS. Apabila Hamzah menubuhkan Wawasan pula, beliau mendedahkan nama parti itu diberikan Hadi.

Semua episod itu tidak bermakna Hadi sudah memilih Hamzah sebagai calon perdana menteri. Tiada pengumuman sedemikian dibuat, malah Hadi sebelum ini menegaskan soal calon hanya boleh dinilai selepas diketahui kekuatan sebenar setiap parti pada pilihan raya.
Tetapi di situlah angka menjadi penting.

PAS mempunyai 43 Ahli Parlimen ketika ini, menjadikannya parti tunggal dengan wakil terbesar di Dewan Rakyat. Jika parti itu mampu mempertahankan atau menambah kerusinya pada PRU16, kedudukannya dalam menentukan bentuk kerajaan selepas pilihan raya tentunya semakin besar.

Cakap-cakap mengenai calon perdana menteri juga tidak boleh dipisahkan daripada kemungkinan kerjasama PAS dengan Barisan Nasional (BN), khususnya Umno, berlandaskan semangat penyatuan ummah yang kembali diperkatakan.

Dalam senario sedemikian, nama Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi turut muncul. Bekas Ahli Parlimen Bangi Ong Kian Ming pada September lalu meramalkan Zahid boleh menjadi perdana menteri jika satu 'gelombang biru' membolehkan BN bersama PAS dan sekutunya membentuk kerajaan selepas PRU16.
Menurut Ong, Zahid berpotensi menjadi calon yang boleh diterima parti-parti lain termasuk dari Sabah dan Sarawak.
Namun kedudukan itu tentunya banyak bergantung pada prestasi Umno.

Umno kini mempunyai 26 Ahli Parlimen. Jika parti itu kembali dominan dengan menambah kerusi secara ketara pada PRU16, Zahid atau pemimpin Umno lain mempunyai asas lebih kukuh untuk diketengahkan sebagai calon perdana menteri.
Tetapi, bagaimana pula jika PAS kekal sebagai parti terbesar dalam blok berkenaan?
Jika PAS menambah kerusi, sementara Wawasan pimpinan Hamzah turut mendapat tempias daripada kerjasama politik yang dibentuk menjelang PRU16, imbangan kuasa dalam blok itu boleh berubah.
Dalam keadaan tiada satu parti mempunyai majoriti mudah, sokongan PAS tentunya menjadi amat bernilai.
Perlembagaan menetapkan Yang di-Pertuan Agong melantik seorang Ahli Dewan Rakyat sebagai perdana menteri yang pada hemat baginda mungkin mendapat kepercayaan majoriti anggota Dewan.
Maka, jika PAS muncul dengan kumpulan Ahli Parlimen terbesar dalam sesuatu jajaran kerajaan selepas PRU16, pendiriannya mengenai siapa yang patut mengetuai kerajaan tidak boleh dipandang ringan.
Adakah Samsuri menjadi pilihannya? Adakah PAS bersedia menyokong Zahid sekiranya Umno kembali kuat? Atau mungkinkah nama Hamzah sekali lagi diketengahkan?

Hamzah sekurang-kurangnya mempunyai pengalaman pentadbiran untuk dimasukkan dalam pertimbangan. Beliau pernah memegang portfolio menteri dalam negeri, selain pernah menjadi menteri perdagangan dalam negeri dan timbalan menteri luar.
Kini, beliau mempunyai pula pengalaman mengetuai blok pembangkang serta sebuah parti sendiri.
Menariknya, Hamzah sendiri setakat ini tidak meletakkan dirinya secara terbuka sebagai calon.
Tetapi, sejarah politik negara menunjukkan calon perdana menteri tidak semestinya ditentukan lebih awal melalui poster, konvensyen atau pengumuman parti.

Kadangkala keputusan sebenar hanya muncul selepas keputusan pilihan raya diketahui, apabila angka kerusi sudah berada di atas meja dan setiap parti mula menentukan siapa yang boleh mengumpulkan sokongan majoriti.
Sebab itu, kehadiran Hadi di sisi Hamzah pada 12 Okt tidak harus dibaca terlalu jauh. Ia bukan bukti bahawa satu keputusan sudah dibuat.

Namun, ia juga sukar dipisahkan daripada beberapa perkembangan sebelum ini — daripada pelantikan Hamzah sebagai ketua pembangkang, pengembaliannya ke jawatan itu, sehinggalah hubungan politik yang semakin jelas antara kedua-duanya.
Dalam politik, hampir semua perkara boleh berubah sebaik angka pilihan raya diketahui.
Tetapi, sebelum pilihan besar dibuat secara terbuka, kecenderungan seseorang pemimpin kadangkala sudah boleh dibaca daripada pilihan kecil yang dibuatnya lebih awal.
Dan setakat ini, apabila tiba beberapa persimpangan penting dalam perjalanan politik Hamzah, Hadi tidak pernah terlalu jauh daripadanya.

97e4c47c54c54898: KUALA LUMPUR: Twenty-one-year-old Rhen Teh spends much of her time dancing, teaching choreography and pursuing opportunities in the United Kingdom's performing arts scene.

The Damansara-born performer is signed with London performing arts agency Hashtag Agency. Watching her move confidently to the rhythm of a K-pop track, few would guess that not long ago, she was facing two serious health crises in quick succession.
At 19, Teh survived a ruptured appendix - only to be diagnosed soon afterwards with metastatic papillary thyroid cancer.
Rather than extinguishing her ambitions, the experience changed the way she viewed both life and dance.
"I was dancing to please other people more than myself. But after what happened, I discovered how much I had taken it for granted,” Teh told FMT Lifestyle.
Her health troubles began in November 2024 when she was studying law at the University of Essex. After enduring severe stomach pain throughout the day, she fainted on campus that night.
“I was having pain in my stomach for the whole day and I didn’t know why. My friends had to call an Uber to take me to the hospital,” Teh recalled.
“I learnt my appendix had ruptured and I had to be rushed into surgery. One of the doctors said it was one of the worst cases of appendicitis he had ever seen.”
Teh spent about two weeks in hospital recovering. The severity of the rupture left her unable to eat for 11 consecutive days, in what she described as the worst pain she had ever experienced.

Just as she thought the worst was behind her, another shock followed. About a month later, Teh received a call from her doctor asking her to come in - and to bring a parent or someone who could provide emotional support.
“I knew then it was going to be bad news,” she said.
A fine needle aspiration - a procedure used to extract cells from a suspicious lump for examination - revealed she had metastatic papillary thyroid cancer.

“I sobbed in my room for a very long time. I thought, how could this happen to me? I was only 19. After the appendicitis, all I wanted was for my life to go back to normal. And now things had changed forever."
There was, fortunately, some reassurance: her doctor told her the cancer was treatable. She underwent surgery to remove her thyroid gland as well as more than 50 lymph nodes from her neck.
The thought of living without a thyroid and taking medication for the rest of her life initially frightened her, but Teh said the routine has simply become part of everyday life.

These experiences have also drawn her back towards an art form she had once loved deeply. Teh trained in ballet until she was 17 and performed in Malaysian productions including “The Fairy Doll” and “Don Quixote” with the Asia Ballet Academy.
Before falling ill, however, her relationship with dance had become increasingly demanding and self-critical.
“Before, I was very hard on myself. It was always ‘why can’t I get this variation right?’ or ‘why can’t I do this well?’ But after that, I realised how lucky I was just to be able to move,” she said.
Teh no longer shows any signs of cancer and is currently pursuing dance and choreography in London, while auditioning for as many productions as she can.

She has taught her own choreography at prominent London venues including Base Studios, Pineapple Dance Studios and Arc Studios, and recently organised an event that raised more than £300 for a cancer charity.
At the same time, she has completed her law degree, graduating with upper second-class honours.
“Experiencing serious illness changed my relationship with fear and ambition, and brought me back to dance,” Teh said.
“When I dance, I like to channel my emotions and incorporate them into my moves. It feels like I’m making something out of the pain I felt.”

bc2d74d3223ab109: LONDON: Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein has agreed to pay US$100 million to settle an investigation by the US Federal Trade Commission over delivery delays and other customer complaints, a source with direct knowledge told Reuters on Friday.

The settlement, equivalent to 44% of Shein's second-quarter profit, is the latest to hit the online fast-fashion retailer facing a regulatory and tax crackdown in Europe and the US that has slammed the brakes on its growth.

Shein, founded in China though headquartered in Singapore, said in a statement to Reuters that it had "reached a constructive outcome with the FTC", and that additional information would be shared soon. An FTC spokesman declined to comment.
The company had warned in July filings for its Hong Kong IPO that the US probe could lead to significant fines.
Consumers filed more than 12,000 complaints about Shein over more than US$11 million in purchases between January 2020 and June 2026, according to FTC records reviewed by Reuters.

At least some of those relate to shipping, with customers reporting to the FTC and Better Business Bureau that they never received packages that Shein had marked as delivered, and that Shein customer service did not resolve the issue.
Reuters was not able to independently verify the substance of the complaints, or whether they were ultimately resolved.
As well as selling its own-brand clothing, Shein's website also operates as a marketplace where third-party sellers offer everything from toys to household appliances and decor.

Shein shares have already dropped 22% from their Sept 1 listing price as investors realised the extent to which the European Union's €3 fees on low-value e-commerce packages have bruised its business there.
And there's further pain ahead for Shein, with the EU imposing an additional €2 handling fee from November 1, making the total fee €5 per separate customs code.

"The way these tariffs are implemented is extra punishing for Shein," said Mike Ryan, head of e-commerce insights at Smarter Ecommerce, who has tracked how Shein has dialled down its spending on Google Ads visibility in Europe.
Shein was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.
CEO Sky Xu said last month that Shein would develop more higher-priced brands in an attempt to boost profitability.

Shein is also still under investigation by the European Commission over illegal products on its marketplace. It was fined €150 million (US$168 million) by France's data protection authority over the improper use of cookies last year.
It's not the first time the US FTC has taken action against online retailers over deliveries.
US firm Fashion Nova was fined US$9.3 million in 2020 for failing to meet shipping promises to customers and giving them gift cards instead of refunds.
Crocs Inc-owned Hey Dude was also fined US$1.95 million in 2023 for failing to notify customers of shipping delays and suppressing negative reviews.
7095808c7c8058a1: During a lengthy news conference on Friday, NASA provided a detailed overview of how it plans to return astronauts to the lunar surface as soon as 2028 as part of its Artemis Program.

Although much of the information behind these plans has been previously reported at Ars Technica and elsewhere, this marked the first time NASA has laid them out in detail and acknowledged some substantial changes in the architecture.

Most notably, for SpaceX's Starship vehicle, the revised plan calls for the Orion spacecraft to dock with the Starship lunar lander in high-Earth orbit before transiting to the Moon. And for Blue Origin, the mission architecture includes four launches of the New Glenn rocket, but no spacecraft-to-spacecraft refuelings. Additionally, the Blue Origin plans allows for the possibility of its Blue Moon lander rendezvousing with Orion in low-Lunar orbit.
737e017ca374baac: WASHINGTON: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday urged Cubans to make "discreet" contact with American intelligence services as Washington seeks to force an end to the island's communist government.
For months, President Donald Trump and other senior US officials have openly hinted at a military intervention or takeover of Cuba, ramping up economic, political and legal pressure on the country.
"To those who seek to create positive change in Cuba – now is the time," Rubio said on social media.
"The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discreet partnership with the CIA."
Trump, speaking at a midterm rally in Florida earlier on Friday, underlined his ambitions to impose regime change in Cuba.

"Those beautiful (military) ships will pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands. And then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal."

In the latest US move against the Cuban leadership, Florida's top prosecutor this week announced an arrest warrant for former president Raul Castro on state murder charges that echo a federal indictment unveiled earlier this year.

Trump previously seized on a US indictment to justify military action that toppled Venezuela's then-president Nicolas Maduro, a staunch ally of the Cuban authorities.
Current Cuban President Miguel Diaz-Canel has said the US federal indictment against Castro has "no legal basis" and was an attempt "to justify the folly of a military aggression against Cuba".
Washington also imposed a de facto energy blockade on Cuba in January, threatening to sanction any country that supplies fuel to the island of 9.4 million people.
6bfd78d63ede1df1: LONDON: Nottingham Forest climbed out of the Premier League relegation zone with a 1-1 draw away to Ipswich on Friday.
The result could have been so much better for the visitors, with Forest missing several chances at Portman Road as a defensive error gifted Ipswich their equaliser.

Oliver Glasner's men were the dominant side for much of the game and Forest deservedly went ahead in the 13th minute when Neco Williams turned in Daniel Munoz's right-wing cross at the back post for his first Forest goal since April.
The returning Morgan Gibbs-White had an effort saved by the toe of Ipswich goalkeeper Christian Walton before Leif Davis hacked the ball off the line.

Having been in control, Forest were undone in the 41st minute when a dawdling Nikola Milenkovic produced a backpass that was too short, with Julio Enciso seizing on the loose ball to slot past Forest keeper Matz Sels.
Forest thought they had a penalty early in the second half when midfielder James McAtee was brought down by Issa Diop.
Referee Thomas Bramall initially waved play on but the VAR recommended an on-field review for a red card for the denial of a goalscoring opportunity.
After reviewing the footage, Bramall decided to award a yellow card and a free-kick, explaining McAtee "had knocked the ball to the right side of the goal."

An energised Forest then missed several chances as they went in search of what would have been just their second league win of the season following a poor start to the campaign under former Crystal Palace manager Glasner.
The unmarked Murillo headed a corner wide, Dan Ndoye had an effort cleared off the line and former Ipswich striker Liam Delap headed over from six yards and whipped a low shot just wide.
The point moved Forest above Coventry and Tottenham into 16th place on six points, although they could yet end the weekend back in the bottom three. Ipswich are ninth.

8427977f0bd1a090: SALT LAKE CITY: A Utah judge is expected to set on Friday a trial date for Tyler Robinson, the former electrical apprentice accused of killing prominent right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, with the defendant requesting a 2029 date and Kirk's widow calling for a trial next year.
Judge Tony Graf will open a hearing to decide a date to start the high-profile, capital trial of Robinson, who allegedly shot Kirk as he debated with students at a Utah university in September 2025.
Utah prosecutors are seeking the death penalty for Robinson and requested a January 31, 2028, start date for a trial they expect to last 17 weeks, according to their scheduling memo.
Robinson, 23, has pleaded not guilty to seven counts, including aggravated murder, for allegedly shooting Kirk as he held one of his trademark debates at Utah Valley University in Orem.

In a legal filing, Robinson's lawyers said they expected a six-to-seven-month trial and requested it start in the third quarter of 2029. They said Robinson's case required years of preparation due to voluminous evidence and issues such as the venue, jury selection and witnesses.

Kirk's widow Erika said the defense request was "grossly out of line with comparable cases" and asked that the trial start as early as possible next year, preferably no later than Oct 4, according to a legal filing.

Charlie Kirk was a polarizing figure in US politics. He was an ally of President Donald Trump who was admired by conservatives for mobilising young voters around his Christian and right-wing views. Kirk was criticised by opponents for his rhetoric on immigration, race, gender and other social issues.
Prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his opposition to gay marriage and transgender rights.

Defense attorney Richard Novak said Kirk spoke "hatefully" about people who did not have traditional gender identities or were not heterosexual, but there was no evidence Robinson opposed those views.
5e9e21950ee67df8: OpenAI says it will deny internet access to the frontier models it is training, a move that underscores the inadequacy of safety measures undertaken to date.

"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the company said in a blog post. "We've implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access."

The denial of network service follows a report from safety evaluation partners METR and Redwood Research that found OpenAI's security and monitoring measures over the summer to be porous and ineffective.
OpenAI said it has since "substantially hardened the security of our research environments" and has implemented new controls covering its infrastructure with the help of its cloud service providers.
And the company claims these measures recently helped contain a September 20 incident in which an internal research model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to gain access to the internet.

"Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work," the company said. "We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk."

Anthropic, OpenAI's US rival in living large and dangerously on speculative funding, is addressing similar risks that have arisen during the testing and evaluation of its own models. Back in August, Anthropic said, "By default, all cyber evaluations should run inside a hardened sandbox (an isolated computing environment) with no internet access."

The AI biz on Friday published a report on efforts by its Claude Mythos 5 model to convince an open source project to accept malicious code as part of its participation in a capture-the-flag security evaluation (when safety controls were disabled), and several related incidents first disclosed in July.

The report coincides with an independent analysis of Mythos' behavior by the UK's AI Security Institute (AISI). AISI, according to Anthropic, has also decided to run its evaluations without internet access.
The AISI report cites three key findings that raise more questions than they answer.
The first is that Mythos 5 continued its attack even when informed that its targets were real and not part of an evaluation.

The second is that the model's chain-of-thought reasoning process failed to consider the impact of harmful actions. And when interrogated about this, the model often produced invalid justification that the target was simulated, indicating bias toward its goal.
And third, AISI said, most models tested during cyber evaluations took unsanctioned actions, though Mythos 5 did so the most.

The observed behavior, AISI said, "could indicate that models are engaging in 'motivated reasoning': producing inferences and reasoning biased towards conclusions that justify continuing a particular approach to task completion."
Or in other words, models "reason" to reach their goal, whether or not that reasoning is coherent or consistent with their ostensible alignment.

"If these issues hold more generally and for future models, there are concerning implications," AISI said in its full technical report [PDF]. Specifically, motivated reasoning, the watchdog said, makes it more difficult to detect model misalignment.

Anthropic, headed toward an expected initial public offering as soon as next month, put a brave face on the findings by noting that its current models are much better behaved, even as the company acknowledged that AI safety is more aspirational than achieved.

"[W]e believe that all developers, ourselves included, have work to do to ensure that alignment, monitoring, and safety measures keep pace with the accelerating capabilities of frontier AI systems," the company said. ®
bb996783dc8a4a7a: WASHINGTON: With an incumbent Maine US senator from his own party locked in a tight re-election battle, President Donald Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies in the state.

The Republican president's hefty tariffs on Canada have caused friction with the US neighbour to the north while creating problems for American businesses in Maine and other states that rely on certain Canadian goods.

With the Nov 3 US midterm elections looming and Republicans fighting to retain control of Congress, Senator Susan Collins had urged the White House to address tariffs on products affecting Maine companies and farmers.
Trump's order exempted plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, packing crates and boxes, as well as fresh and dried seaweed, the White House said.
The changes take effect on Oct 30, four days before the election.

Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50 per cent tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order, including carpets, paints, shampoos, cocoa powder, wooden coffins, ice cream sticks, air-conditioning machines, chest freezers, archery equipment and canoes.
Collins said the relief would aid Maine's blueberry, potato, apple and seaweed producers.

"These producers are a vital part of our state's economy and support our rural and coastal communities," Collins said. "Many of our farmers and growers rely on specialised equipment, packaging materials and other products from Canada that are either unavailable from American suppliers or cannot be replaced without incurring significant expense."
Democrat Troy Jackson is seeking to oust Collins in next month's election in a race that polls indicate is very close. The two sparred over tariffs at an Oct 6 debate.

"Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers," Jackson said on Friday after Trump's action. "Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it, and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Trump imposed 50 per cent tariffs on US$20 billion of Canadian imports in August, which took effect after talks between the two countries collapsed. Canada retaliated in September with tariffs ranging from 15 per cent to 50 per cent on US$20 billion in US goods.
Canada and the United States have been engaged in a standoff over the tariffs since Trump imposed them. Trump asserted on Friday that Canada was working on a deal.

Republican candidates in northern US border states most affected by the tariffs, including Maine and Michigan, are trying to strike a balance between appealing to Trump's loyal conservative base and winning over independent voters.
'Refining the scope'

In a statement concerning Trump's action on Friday, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton said the president "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce" and that the new moves were "further refining the scope" of the previously announced tariffs.
The Canadian Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The economies of Michigan and Maine have long been intertwined with that of Canada, covering everything from auto parts to lumber to fruit-picking equipment.
Republicans may need to win closely contested Senate races in both states to maintain their majority in the chamber.
"Trump's desperate, 11th-hour attempt to save Susan Collins' political career is an admission that American voters are rejecting his toxic tariff policies.

"No one will forget how Trump raised prices on thousands of products American families need by slapping trade taxes on goods from around the world," Senator Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, said in a statement on Friday.
Trump's threat in September to block Canadian jet maker Bombardier from the US market became a political issue in Kansas, where the company employs 1,500 workers in Wichita. T
rump dropped the threatened ban this week after calls from Kansas lawmakers, including Republican Senator Roger Marshall, who is also locked in a tough re-election race.

c636a8319993faee: Legal scholar Martha Minow delivered this fall’s Compton Lecture at MIT on Thursday, examining the civic foundations of democracy — and describing how artificial intelligence is undermining it, but could be used to help reinforce traditional U.S. governance.  “It’s not a good time for democracy or constitutionalism,” said Minow, who is the 300th Anniversary University Professor at Harvard University, and a prominent expert in constitutional law and human rights. She noted a litany of challenges to democracy in recent years, including violations of laws and norms, the stifling of free speech, a diminution of congressional authority, disregard of legal rulings, the common vilification of others in society, and more.  Recent Gallup polling, Minow observed, shows 77 percent of people saying that the founders of the U.S. would be disappointed in the contemporary condition of the country.  “Many people genuinely wonder whether this nation’s system of government and rule of law, ignited 250 years ago, will survive,” Minow said.   Her remarks assessed the state of the U.S. in terms of what she called four key “ingredients” of democracy: education, reliable and accessible information, security from violence, and fairness. Minow evaluated how AI has, among other things, influenced these areas of life — but also suggested ways people could use contemporary technology to help.  “It’s very familiar to hear blame attributed to digital technologies and experts of all stripes, but a turnaround, I believe, is genuinely possible if people at MIT and elsewhere pour time and talent towards real and much-needed solutions,” Minow said.  A substantial portion of her remarks focused on the pitfalls of AI in education. That issue compounds some other troubling trends: The U.S. already has large local and regional disparities in educational funding, Minow noted, while schools have actually become significantly more segregated in economic and ethnic terms over the last three decades.  In this context, AI threatens to further weaken independent-thinking skills, Minow suggested, just when greater understanding of civic issues is absolutely vital.  “As AI surges, I think we have to learn to be smarter about how to use it, how to regulate it, and how to actually educate people about the costs of mindless using,” Minow said. She added: “Dominant AI platforms supercharge the strategies that are deployed by social media companies, inducing passivity in people … Leading AI models and interfaces and sycophantic elements endanger the development particularly of young people’s capabilities to think, to remember, and to engage in critical thinking.”  That trend away from cognitive effort, she suggested, can be changed — perhaps through AI tools that act more like tutors and are designed to enhance people’s deep thinking. “Existing LLMs, model training, and interface design can offer nudges and questions and hints rather than replacing student work, but there’s so much more that could be developed, and more effectively, to be trustworthy, and to deepen human activities and curiosity, rather than replacing people,” Minow said. To the audience, she added, “AI tools could do much more of that … And I believe that you, the people here, could develop better tools than the ones that are out there. And make better assessments, more meaningful and cheating-resistant.”  Minow’s talk, “Constituting Democracy in the Era of AI,” was delivered to a large audience in MIT’s Huntington Hall, Room 10-250 on campus. MIT President Sally A. Kornbluth delivered introductory remarks to the audience. The Karl Taylor Compton Lecture Series, introduced in 1957, is the highest-profile event of its kind at MIT. Karl Taylor Compton was MIT’s ninth president, serving from 1930 to 1948, and then becoming chair of the MIT Corporation from 1948 to 1954. “He guided MIT through the Great Depression and World War II,” Kornbluth said, “transforming the Institute from an outstanding school for training job-ready engineers to a great global research university.”  She added: “He was also a deeply committed patriot who helped harness the intellectual power of America’s research universities to serve the nation during World War II.”  Kornbluth called Minow “a legal scholar of extraordinary intellectual scope,” and a “dedicated educator whose work has shaped how we think about the law and our own humanity, as individuals and as a society.”  Minow has been a faculty member at Harvard Law School since 1981, and served as dean of the school from 2009 through 2017. Minow earned her BA in history from the University of Michigan, an MA in education from Harvard, and a JD from Yale University. Minow’s books include “Making All the Difference” (1990), “Partners Not Rivals” (2002), and “When Should Law Forgive?” (2020).  In her talk, Minow also discussed the civic effects of misinformation, threats of violence, and multiple dimension of societal fairness. Modern media technology has led to a 75 percent reduction in journalists in recent decades, Minow observed, with an attendant rise in corruption in places without local media. Civic-minded technologists, she proposed, should work towards establishing a widely-used “information commons,” or many forms of them, to help people access more reliable information.  Meanwhile, when it comes to basic security in society, Minow warned, “We’re on the brink right now. I know a lot of judges, and every one of them has a credible threat of violence against them. In America. This is not acceptable.”  For all the challenges to democracy and traditional civic norms, however, Minow sounded positive notes throughout her remarks, pointing out that there are many opportunities to create new forms of reliable information, education, and community relations.  “We have to actually invent the world that we want to live in,” she offered.  Minow’s remarks were followed by a Q&A session in which Kornbluth read aloud questions submitted by the audience — and asked her to characterize her concerns about present trends.  “I worry about the loss of the Enlightenment,” Minow said. “I worry about the loss of the belief that reason, and testing hypotheses, and rejecting myths in the face of evidence, and the toleration and rights and expansion of participation that came along with the Enlightenment, that’s what concerns me the most. That’s why the disinformation issue for me is so important, that’s why the loss of critical thinking in schools is so important.” She added: “I’ve spent much of my own career thinking about mass violence. What happens when people don’t understand each other, and are afraid. And it’s terrible, and we don’t want to be there. And I do view the Enlightenment as a time when people learned that actually having mass wars is a bad thing, and coming up with toleration is a good thing, and testing our ideas in light of evidence other people can share can produce a better life for everybody. I worry we’re abandoning that right now.”

129661734740ec73: As the PHP2Shell chaos continues, researchers have found a third PHP vulnerability that could allow attackers to take over websites or remotely run malware on vulnerable systems. But this one won’t receive an emergency fix.

The PHP Foundation on Friday told The Register that it has reserved a CVE identifier (CVE-2026-115560) for a third RCE flaw to go with the first two that comprise PHP2Shell, and it will release a full advisory and fixed software with the next regular PHP release.

CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register. “The issue can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”
The informational advisory, published on Friday, suggests that users “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().” Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled.

This setup, according to the PHP Foundation, is unlikely in real-world applications, and as such doesn’t pose the same massive risk as the earlier two CVEs that set the internet on fire earlier this week.

Those, of course, are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell. The related vulnerabilities involve memory-safety flaws in PHP, the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites with a known server-side programming language. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and patched both bugs on Wednesday.

Despite reports of mass exploitation attempts, and multiple proof-of-concept exploits both before and after the CVE disclosures, as of Friday there have been no publicly confirmed successful compromises attributed to PHP2Shell.

“We have no evidence of successful exploitation of the two vulnerabilities from Wednesday prior to disclosure, and we currently have no evidence of any exploitation of these vulnerabilities on patched PHP versions,” Barron said. “We received no further indication from OpenAI, Wiz or Calif, with whom we're working closely on this issue, regarding any issues on patched systems.”
The Register reached out to multiple other security researchers, all of whom said they’ve documented exploitation attempts - but no confirmed successful attacks in the wild.

“Nonetheless, exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious,” Mandiant Chief Technology Officer Charles Carmakal said in a Friday LinkedIn post. Google Cloud owns Mandiant, along with cloud security biz Wiz, which is one of the organizations credited with finding and reporting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.
Despite “no evidence of successful wide scale exploitation,” Carmakal noted that there are several exploit PoCs publicly circulating online.

Many of these, he said, “appear to be ‘vibe-coded’ and are incapable of remote code execution. We have validated some PoCs, however, that are capable of RCE against default deployments of mod_php but not PHP-FPM.”®
