690aea53d2bd1733: Generative artificial intelligence models are rooted in ideas of mid-20th century engineers who thought some amount of irrationality was essential for a machine that could think like a human, contends Benjamin Lindquist, an assistant professor in the MIT History Section, who holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems.  To mimic creative thinking, these AI pioneers intentionally injected randomness into algorithms designed to deterministically solve problems, Lindquist writes in a new paper that appears in the journal Past and Present. In the paper, he traces the origins of AI hallucinations back to this early research and suggests there will be inevitable tradeoffs between creativity and predictability when trying to build machines that mimic human behavior. MIT News spoke with Lindquist about these ideas. Q: Why did early computer engineers believe they needed to inject randomness and irrationality into AI systems designed for logic and calculation?  A: There is a long history of many figures in the world of science and art theorizing that chance plays an important part in discovery and creativity — in the ability to originate ideas. They equated creativity with unexpected leaps of logic, or even a dream-like state that allows you to think about things from a new perspective.  In the early 1950s, one popular idea from John Pierce, who was a prominent electrical engineer at Bell Labs, was about math being valuable in the world of art. The idea was shared by a lot of people working in early computing. When we think of artwork that includes math, we may think of something very orderly and precise, but Pierce came to the opposite conclusion. He concluded that the utility of math is that it could remove order from art. Then in a very calculated way, math could add a burst of the unexpected as a means to deviate from clichés and add an element of irregularity which just might lead to insight.  One popular way to add irregularity into otherwise predictable computers was through artificial (or random) neural networks. Many early neural networks were built by psychologists, who thought that by enabling scientists to build a model of the brain, artificial neural networks allowed scientists to observe what is happening inside, including how brains make productive mistakes. Rather than being black boxes, researchers believed these systems could open this black box of the mind and let scientists peer inside and see all the messy stuff that was really happening. But there was another camp in the world of AI who thought that creative thinking was just “normal” thinking done better. It is interesting to look at these two very simplistic heuristics for understanding intelligence and creativity, and how they do and don’t mesh. The debate, then, was about trying to determine what human inventiveness boils down to, and then how to reconstitute human inventiveness in machine form.  Q: How did these early computer engineers view AI, and how is it different from the way we think about AI today? A: When we think of AI systems, we think of ChatGPT or Claude. We value and use these systems because they give answers that, most of the time, are correct. One of the things that was most interesting to me in this research was finding out that a lot of the early advocates of these systems valued them for exactly the opposite reason. They wanted a system that, on occasion, gave answers that deviated from their expectations. They already had systems that could deliver reasonable and expected answers. They saw neural networks as valuable because they could give unexpected, perhaps even strange and bizarre answers. One reason we might view these systems differently today could be because of how they operate. Early on, these systems were confined to laboratories, so there weren’t really any real-world consequences of a system that gives a strange, or wrong, output. But now there are legal and monetary reasons why OpenAI or Anthropic doesn’t want a chatbot that gives unexpected or creative answers. There has been a “sanding down” of strangeness in these systems. They still potentially have that at their core, but it is something that is now largely suppressed. Q: How did early neural networks that incorporated randomness to simulate human creativity evolve to become the dominant paradigm in AI? A: For a long time, a specific kind of AI called “symbolic AI” was the dominant approach. Essentially, symbolic AI says the world is based on rules. The role of the AI researcher is to try and reconstruct the knowledge of the world in facts and propositions and feed it into a computer. Neural networks, with their use of randomness to solve problems, started to gain traction in the 1950s but fell out favor early on. Frank Rosenblatt, a psychologist who was a very important early figure in neural networks, died prematurely; he died accidentally on his 43rd birthday in 1971. He was quite a charismatic and forceful personality, who made a lot of grand promises about what systems based on neural networks could do. By the time he died, a shift toward symbolic AI was already underway. It is possible if, had he lived, things might have turned out differently. But neural networks never went away. By the 1980s they had shifted more into the world of cognitive science. To become more powerful, and more useful, neural networks needed a lot of data and computational power. That didn’t really arrive until the advent of the internet, when a lot of data became available and computing started to power up. Around 2012, neural networks started to outperform and outpace a statistical form of machine learning, and they kept growing from there. Q: What lessons can we learn from studying AI’s history that could inform its development?  A: I think there is a cautionary lesson here. The ideas and experiences of these early engineers tell us that we can work toward quashing hallucinations — we can work toward making AI perform a certain way so it doesn’t produce unexpected or unwanted answers — but there are going to be other consequences of that. These historical figures were onto something. There is a connection between the surprising and creative conclusions AI can offer and errors or hallucinations. There are tradeoffs when we build our systems to behave one way or the other. Maybe it is impossible to be completely at either end of the spectrum, but when we work toward one thing robustly, we often sacrifice something else unintentionally.
291f0719d1e3f06f: "Malaysians asked to remove haze, government asking to remove Waze". Satu lagi berbunyi, "ask government to settle haze, they got rid of Waze". Tak tahu siapa yang mencipta ungkapan itu tetapi dia memang creative buat lawak sinis.

Ada rhyme 'haze' dengan 'Waze'. Kata-kata itu sudah mendapat tempat di pelbagai platform media sosial. Saya sendiri tersenyum lebar membacanya. Ini susulan tindakan kerajaan melarang penjawat awam menggunakan aplikasi navigasi Waze berkuat kuasa serta-merta. Walaupun larangan membabitkan hanya kakitangan kerajaan, orang ramai turut digalakkan berhenti guna Waze.
Oleh kerana jerebu masih bersama kita, terciptalah jenaka sinis 'haze' dan 'waze' yang disebut tadi. Namun jika diambil kira alasan kerajaan, this is no laughing matter.

Kata Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim, tindakan diambil bagi melindungi maklumat kerajaan dan data peribadi pengguna yakni penjawat awam daripada ancaman penyalahgunaan oleh rejim Israel. Keputusan dibuat PMX dengan mengambil kira kedudukan Waze Mobile Ltd sebagai pengawal data pengguna yang diperbadankan dan beroperasi di bawah undang-undang Israel.

Berkata pula Menteri Digital Gobind Singh Deo, "jika melihat dokumen perjanjian (sebelum mengaktifkan aplikasi) kita bersetuju dengan syarat-syarat tertentu iaitu di bawah bidang kuasa undang-undang Israel dan itu menjadi satu masalah kepada kita."

Majlis Keselamatan Negara pula kata tiada kompromi terhadap sebarang risiko keselamatan melibatkan Israel. Reaksi Waze ialah menafikan aplikasinya mengumpulkan maklumat sensitif kerajaan atau membenarkan pihak ketiga mengeksplotasi data peribadi pengguna. Penafian ini memang dijangkakan.
Larangan kerajaan stands. Ketua Pengarah MKN Raja Nushirwan Zainal Abidin berkata penjawat awam yang melanggar arahan boleh dikenakan tindakan tatatertib.

Saya percaya ramai dalam kalangan ribuan penjawat awam menggunakan Waze. Yang membingungkan saya bagaimana mahu memastikan semua yang menggunakan Waze mematuhi arahan. Adakah setiap penjawat awam akan diperiksa seorang demi seorang? Mengambil kira bilangan kakitangan awam yang guna Waze, pelaksanaan arahan tentunya bukan mudah.
Kata MKN, "dari segi pelaksanaan arahan ada caranya tetapi secara umum kita serahkan kepada ketua jabatan masing-masing". That is not saying much.
Oleh kerana jutaan rakyat menggunakan Waze tentunya larangan kerajaan menarik perhatian ramai.

Pertanyaan ramai ialah why now? Mungkinkah berdasarkan informasi terkini? Jika penggunaan Waze mengancam keselamatan negara dan diri sendri apa lagi yang mengancam ialah Israel, mengapa larangan tidak menyeluruh dan membabitkan semua rakyat, meskipun saya akui ini akan menyebabkan kesulitan.

Menurut Raja Nushirwan, kerajaan mengambil pendekatan berfasa berteraskan pendidikan awam demi mengimbangi tuntutan keselamatan dan kebebasan memilih rakyat. Maka sekarang eloklah kita tunggu 'pendidikan awam' yang beliau katakan. Dalam bentuk apa agaknya ia akan disalurkan kepada rakyat?
"Dengan cara yang kita ambil ini kita serahkan kepada rakyat Malaysia untuk memilih secara sendiri," kata beliau. Terima kasih. Rakyat lain ada pilihan sendiri, tidak seperti penjawat awam.

Menurut Anwar, kerajaan menggalakkan orang ramai untuk menggunakan aplikasi tempatan, TuJu, yang dibangunkan oleh Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia sebagai alternatif bagi keperluan navigasi jalan raya. Jujur saya kata saya tidak tahu akan kewujudan TuJu. Pun begitu semasa menonton Buletin Utama tiga malam lalu, beberapa warganegara yang sudah lama menggunakan TuJu rata-rata puas hati dengan prestasi aplikasi itu.
Apabila Anwar mencadangkan orang ramai guna TuJu, ramai menyambut saranan beliau. Ada lonjakan ketara jumlah pengguna TuJu selepas PMX mengesyorkan pengunaannya. That’s on the upside.

On the downside tercetus gangguan teknikal yang menjejaskan perisian navigasi TuJu. Kata Lembaga Lebuhraya Malaysia ia sudah bekerjasama dengan penyedia aplikasi, Prosignal Consortium, untuk mengenal pasti punca gangguan, memulihkan kestabilan sistem serta meningkatkan kapasiti aplikasi bagi menampung jumlah pengguna yang semakin bertambah.

Bercakap mengenai penyedia aplikasi TuJu, macam-macam spekulasi dalam kalangan orang ramai yang saya tidak cadang menghuraikan, sekadar menyatakan memang biasa apabila kerajaan recommend sesuatu perkara, syarikat yang mengendalikannya akan diletak di bawah mikroskop. Kadangkala ada spekulasi betul dan ada yang bohong.

Apapun if there's anything good to come out of this Waze issue, it is proof that Malaysia atau lebih tepat rakyat boleh mencipta aplikasi membanggakan. Jika tidak lebih baik, ia setanding Waze. Semakin ramai kenal TuJu maka cepatlah atasi kesulitan.

a52a4b92f90e0388: In a matter of just over a month, a perfect storm has pushed Zetrix AI Bhd to the precipice of corporate oblivion. In the process, the digital services firm’s share price has crashed by over 90% and its market capitalisation has plummeted by over RM5 billion.

The collapse of its shares started on Aug 27 when it opened at 66 sen, with the company valued at about RM5.33 billion. By the end of the day, the company formerly known as My EG Services Bhd had fallen nearly 10% to 59.5 sen.
The next day, the dam broke when the shares suffered a intraday plunge of 50.4% to close at 29.5 sen, erasing RM2.4 billion from its market value.

The monumental collapse was attributed to speculation linking it with the corruption case of former human resources minister M Saravanan as well as forced selling of the shares of its co-founder and group managing director Wong Thean Soon.

Things got progressively worse with the share price falling like a rock as the bad news piled up. On Oct 5, the Road Transport Department (JPJ) suspended Zetrix and its subsidiary MyEG Sdn Bhd as collection agents over unremitted government revenue.
Transport minister Loke Siew Fook then dropped the bombshell that Zetrix failed to remit RM314 million in collected government revenues.
This prompted the police to open an investigation into the matter, with the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) also jumping into the fray.
The troubles afflicting Zetrix put it firmly in the crosshairs of rating agencies. On Oct 18, 2026, MARC Ratings downgraded its RM2 billion sukuk (Islamic bonds) programme rating to BB+IS from AA-IS.
The stock then tumbled on news of a potential covenant breach looming over the sukuk programme. Under its trust deed, Wong is required to remain Zetrix’s single largest shareholder.

However, his stake has been slashed to just 1.84% currently from nearly 30% following forced share sales by banks triggered by margin calls. The sukuk trustee has given Zetrix until Oct 22 to remedy the issue, which seems highly unlikely given Wong is no longer a substantial shareholder.

This means it needs to seek sukuk holders’ approval for a waiver if the breach is not resolved by then. Without a waiver, the breach could trigger early repayment of the RM2 billion principal as well as RM164.5 million in future coupon payments.
Any default of the sukuk will trigger a Practice Note 17 (PN17) classification. That would be catastrophic for Zetrix.
To aggravate matters, the company announced it was withdrawing its first interim dividend of 0.25 sen per share (amounting to RM19.7 million) for FY2026 declared two months ago to “conserve cash”.

In the face of all the bad press, Zetrix’s share price hit an intraday low of 5 sen last Friday (Oct 16), its lowest level in over 14 years, valuing the company at RM404 million. The stock is within touching distance of its all-time low price of 3.5 sen, which was reached in 2008.
Zetrix’s paradox
Ironically, Zetrix should be trading nearer to its all-time high than its record low, based on its financial results.
For the year ended Dec 31, 2025 (FY2025), its net profit hit RM883.85 million, a 24.9% rise from the previous year, while revenue jumped 31.3% to RM1.34 billion.
Just two days before Zetrix’s selloff started end-August, MBSB Research forecast it would hit RM1.1 billion in core earnings for FY2026.
MBSB noted Zetrix’s normalised earnings for the first half of 2026 jumped 38.9% to RM540.7 million, and was on track to achieve the RM1 billion earnings milestone.
On the face of it, companies having such strong financial performance should not be trading at 5 sen. That is the paradox facing Zetrix.
Its financials are the not the problem, rather it is a crisis of confidence. For Zetrix, restoring confidence in the company is paramount.

Under Wong’s leadership, the group realised its e-government services business model was inherently risky as the need for such a “middleman” was untenable in the long run. The expansion of the MyJPJ app signals the government is increasingly capable of providing digital services directly.

Its name change last year to Zetrix from My EG is a reflection of its strategy of transforming itself from an e-government services provider into a blockchain and artificial intelligence (AI) company.

Its robust financial performance in recent years can be attributed to this transformation. Blockchain and AI-related revenue increased from RM127.6 million in 2023 to RM362.8 million in 2024, and RM643.5 million in 2025.

Its first half FY2026 earnings of over half a billion ringgit was supported by AI subscriptions and services, Web3 application fees and sales of Zetrix Layer-1 nodes. Nevertheless, non-AI and non-blockchain activities still account for about 40% of group revenue.
However, this transformation seems to have become its achilles heels as it has racked up huge debt to roll out the new business.
By end-June 2026, cumulative development expenditure had reached a whopping RM3.7 billion from RM2.85 billion at end-2025. That expenditure is likely to continue growing.

At end-June, Zetrix had RM541.6 million in cash and cash equivalents against RM853.1 million in short-term loans and borrowings. Total borrowings stood at RM2.2 billion, up 74.3% from RM1.26 billion a year earlier.

Its current financial woes may well be linked to the burgeoning debt to finance its investment in blockchain infrastructure, AI applications and international expansion. The question remains whether Zetrix has bitten off more than it can chew?

While the transformation appears to be bearing fruit with rising revenue and earnings, investors and financial institutions want to know if these are recurring and sustainable, given the huge investment involved.
Last throw of the dice

Zetrix may have a trump card to deal with its rising debt and cashflow issues as it is preparing to list its AI and blockchain unit, AI Foundation Lab, on the Nasdaq by end-2026. The plan is even backed by a US$40 million (RM163 million) equity investment from International Finance Corp, the World Bank’s investment arm.

The company is targeting a valuation of US$3 billion (RM12.2 billion) alongside a US$200 million (RM816.3 million) capital-raising exercise before the listing, according to a CLSA note. It plans to eventually pare down its stake in the US-listed company, with proceeds to be used to reduce its debt, and potentially pay a special dividend.

However, these projections were done prior to the brutal selloff, which has thrown a spanner into the works. MARC said its proposed Nasdaq listing could be deferred to the first quarter of 2027 from its initial end-2026 target.
“While the proposed listing could broaden the group’s access to capital, recent developments affecting its business and financial profile could present challenges to its completion,” it said.
It added Zetrix’s reliance on “transactions that remain subject to execution risks” offered limited assurance that funds would be available in time for debt repayment.
This potential Nasdaq listing may well be the last throw of the dice for Wong and Zetrix. If it is executed successfully, they may well be able to prevent the company from falling off the precipice.

ab004f619c0b5081: The renminbi is back at the centre of debates about global macroeconomic imbalances. With China’s merchandise trade surplus widening to US$1.2 trillion in 2025, and with its manufacturing sector becoming increasingly dominant, the near-consensus among financial and economic commentators is that the renminbi is significantly undervalued.

The implication is that China should let its currency appreciate sharply, thereby shrinking its surplus, easing competitive pressure on manufacturers elsewhere, and helping rebalance the global economy.

This argument is politically convenient, because it points to a seemingly painless solution. Unfortunately, it suffers from a fatal flaw. Before simply assuming that exchange-rate appreciation is appropriate for China, one must examine the underlying cause of the currency’s weakness.

If it was primarily the result of deliberate interventions to expand exports, rapid appreciation would indeed be a relatively clean remedy. But if it reflects weak domestic demand, allowing the currency to appreciate without addressing the underlying weakness would be counterproductive.
China falls into the second category. The renminbi’s weakness and the widening surplus are better understood as parallel consequences of a deep adjustment in the real-estate sector.

Property was once a central engine of Chinese demand, credit creation, local-government finance, household wealth, and investment. When the property market suffers, so does domestic demand, particularly investment demand. And when investment falls faster than national saving, the external surplus rises.

China is not unusual in this respect. CF40 Research has identified a clear pattern: housing busts have improved economies’ external balances. That is what happened previously in the US and Japan, where weak domestic demand also led to persistently low inflation.

While the renminbi’s nominal exchange rate has been quite stable against both the US dollar and a basket of currencies in recent years, high global inflation and low domestic inflation have produced a large real depreciation. It is not a weak currency that has undermined domestic demand and led to large external surpluses; it is the opposite.

The renminbi’s exchange rate matters, but how it adjusts matters more. An appreciation driven by an economic recovery would be welcome. If the property sector stabilises, household confidence improves, productive investment rises, and imports grow, the currency would strengthen as part of the broader rebalancing.

But too abrupt an appreciation would not repair China’s property market or revive domestic demand. On the contrary, it would hurt the export sector and the investment and consumption that it supports.
The impact on global imbalances would be ambiguous, but it would almost certainly slow China’s recovery, potentially leading to weaker growth for a world economy that would be no less unbalanced.

The rest of the world therefore has a big stake in how China adjusts. China has become a price anchor for a large part of global manufacturing, since producer prices increasingly shape goods prices elsewhere, even when the final product is not imported directly from China.

In fact, weak Chinese demand and a low renminbi exchange rate have helped restrain goods inflation in advanced economies, though this benefit receives far less attention than the competitive pressure China places on foreign producers.

The post-Covid disinflation in advanced economies was a case in point. It came not only from tighter monetary policies and repaired supply chains, but also from soft Chinese manufactured-goods prices.
Sharp currency appreciation would push in the opposite direction, raising the price of Chinese exports. The result would feel less like a painless rebalancing than a cost-push shock.

Such an adjustment would not promote factory construction in Europe, higher productivity in the US, or improvements in China’s property market. It would simply increase the global prices of manufactured goods at a time when inflation in many advanced economies remains elevated. Some foreign producers might welcome the easing of Chinese competition, but central banks’ job would get harder.

Bond markets would also feel the effects. Expectations of higher inflation and tighter monetary policy would increase pressure on nominal yields at a time when advanced economies are already drawing down global savings.

With the US running large fiscal deficits, Europe preparing for more spending on defense and infrastructure, and AI investments creating enormous demand for capital, the need for savings from the rest of the world has grown.

In this context, one must remember that China’s surplus is the counterpart of Chinese net savings supplied to the rest of the world. If China absorbs more at home, less Chinese savings will be available to finance deficits abroad.
That could drive a healthy adjustment if deficit countries were to save more and borrow less. But failing that, bond yields—which have already climbed to multi-year highs—must continue to rise.
None of this means that China should hold down its currency artificially. Rather, it should try to rebalance by strengthening domestic demand.
That means stabilising the property sector, improving household income expectations, expanding social insurance, and shifting investment towards more productive uses.
Such policies would narrow the surplus more durably than exchange-rate adjustment alone. The renminbi would duly strengthen as the recovery takes hold.

But deficit countries have responsibilities, too. They cannot demand smaller Chinese surpluses while continuing to count on cheap imported goods, disinflationary pressure, and abundant foreign savings. If advanced economies want China to absorb more of what it produces, they must show more fiscal discipline themselves.
Kai Guo is executive president and senior fellow of the CF40 Institute.

Such insubordination would once have meant instant dismissal even for the stellar likes of Roy Keane and David Beckham.
But today, a geological age of anguish later, almost all fans and probably most players feel the complainant is stating the obvious.
For many of the bedraggled army that still follow United in Europe, the sentiment was not for sacking another manager, but for removing the hierarchy.
You would hope that the richest United fans might resort to a revival of the Red Knights that tried to wrest control of the club in 2010.
Mere millionaires came up short last time, but if billionaires were serious, and fans make life difficult for Ratcliffe, you never know.
Beckham is a billionaire now. In 2010, he wore a green and gold scarf to give his support. He needs to rustle up a few rich cronies.
Club captain Fernandes did bring tactics into it, which are at Michael Carrick’s door, but the loathing for the ownership is ratcheting up several notches.
If losing at Atletico Madrid could not be compared to Grimsby or the recent home loss to Brighton after a two-goal lead, Como is in a league of its own.
As recently as 2019, Como were in Italy’s Serie D playing at a communal stadium with a capacity of just over 1,000.
They are managed by Cesc Fabregas, who is remembered as much for throwing pizza at Sir Alex Ferguson as for his spells in midfield with Arsenal and Chelsea.
At the ‘Battle of the Buffet’, it was just a slice; this was the whole pizza, deep-pan with lots of topping.
Como were all over them and United didn’t deserve even a late consolation.
To have progressed to Europe’s premier competition under a rookie manager in that time is a salutary tale for United. Another one.
In between these losses, United managed a creditable draw at Leeds, but they have won only two of ten games this season.
They are a precarious 21st in the Champions League table.
They’re on course for the second-round playoffs, but not a million miles from the ignominy of elimination (positions 25 to 36).
In the EPL, they are 13th, but play Bournemouth, Chelsea, Aston Villa, Arsenal and Liverpool next.
No one is predicting a surge up the table.
We pretty well know what will happen next. Carrick will cling on till December, eking out the odd result.
Jim Ratcliffe will say he’s “fully supportive” while interviewing all the usual suspects.
And so it goes on.
As the fans are all too painfully aware, changing the manager doesn’t work.
With the exception of Tommy Docherty’s five-year reign, United has had only two successful managers since the Second World War.
Matt Busby, appointed in 1945 – delayed while he completed military service – and Fergie in 1986.
Looking at the names post-Fergie, they should have done better. David Moyes is still at it with Everton, having led West Ham to a European trophy.
Louis van Gaal is one of the giants of the era and, despite illness, took the Netherlands to a quarter-final loss on penalties to Argentina in the 2022 World Cup.
He was sacked immediately after winning the FA Cup with United and blames City’s “cheating” for his demise.
Jose Mourinho is now at Real Madrid, but he did win the League Cup and Europa League. United were not that bad in those days.
Ralf Rangnick lasted only months as an interim, but it’s widely accepted that he was “sacked” by Ronaldo.
Where was the hierarchy? Where were the Glazers?
And where were they when Rangnick gave his list of players he wanted United to sign?
Avert your gaze now, United fans, as it could be painful reading. Among them were: Erling Haaland, Luis Diaz, Julian Alvarez, Enzo Fernandez, and Josko Gvardiol.
With those and under his astute guidance – he was mentor to the likes of Jurgen Klopp, Thomas Tuchel and Julian Nagelsmann – United could have outdone City.
And there are two more. Between the outbursts by Martinez and Fernandes, Erik ten Hag took a swipe as well.
The Dutchman revealed that he’d wanted Harry Kane and Declan Rice, but his request fell on deaf ears.
Fergie had famously said he’d suffered more pain dealing with Spurs chairman Daniel Levy than from his hip operation, so chief executive Richard Arnold and football director John Murtough didn’t try.
Even though Kane was desperate for the move!
Ditto West Ham and Rice. The Hammers didn’t want to sell, but Arsenal managed to prise their star asset away a year later for £110m.
With those seven players, United would have had a side to take on the world.
Ten Hag also partly blames City for his sacking, but in the period of City’s illegal £900m spending spree, United matched them almost pound for pound, totally above board.
But the Glazers surpassed that figure, taking out an estimated £1.5 billion in dividends and interest.
Absentee owners, incompetent directors. Enter Ratcliffe and the Politburo.
Where the Glazers treat United as a cash cow, to Ratcliffe it’s a hobby horse.
The billionaire sports fan loves to dabble in several and involves his petrochemical company, INEOS.
But unfortunately for him and his many victims, he has the Sadim touch – the opposite of Midas. Or, what has been dubbed the INEOS Curse.
In football, French club Nice have had seven managers in five years while Swiss club Lausanne suffered relegation before coming back up.
The dominant SKY cycling team lost their way when INEOS took over, as did Mercedes in F1 as soon as INEOS sponsorship came in.
Britain’s America's Cup sailing challenge ended in humiliation and litigation after Ratcliffe took over.
Even the mighty All Blacks suddenly became vulnerable with Ratcliffe’s backing.
Cash cow or hobby horse? Between them, the owners have cooked up a real dog’s breakfast.
It’s time for the Red Knights to ride again.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
4a7fb2460297143f: A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining "userland" access that he says "lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO."

The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called "tethered" hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.

Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI's Codex to poke at SmileBasic's language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After "substantial effort for ~2 weeks," that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read-and-write access to portions of system memory.

d96f1085411f42cd: NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like it is trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes.

712bc0d815dcfe0f: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.

That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”

Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.
Start with the workload, not the model
There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.

A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.
The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.

That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.

A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t.

The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost.
Engineer the system, not the model

Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.

Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.

GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.

The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.

Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements.

For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.
Build for change, not today’s benchmark

Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.

EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.
The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.

88e73b340e5cf3c4: As a child, you likely saw a few Disney movies depicting inanimate objects, such as clocks, cups, and toys, as interactive companions to humans — an act of pure magic, seemingly. But scientists at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) are now doing something similar: transforming stationary items into self-aware tools that perceive and respond to human motion to complete a task. Engineers have 3D-printed these dynamic items with built-in sensing, using conductive materials for sensors and traces (sort of like wires) inside. The issue: both components were typically fabricated using the same material, so they’d emit similar signals. It’s sort of like hearing two radio stations at the same time, a mixup that’s hard to interpret. This confuses, say, a glove that relays instructions to a robotic hand about how to handle a specific object. The device couldn’t filter out the noise or verify the angle of a user’s motions, leading a humanoid student to make errors. Researchers at CSAIL and Tianjin University (TJU) in China may have found a way to 3D print more precise interactive items. With their “X-Hinges” software, users can customize a design, and the tool will automatically embed two different materials: a filament for the sensors designed to send the strongest signal possible, and another for the wire-like elements that don’t interfere. Interactions won’t get lost in translation, meaning users can fabricate objects that respond in real-time, such as small robots, household decor, object-detection systems, and toys. With X-Hinges, users can put together an item by selecting and connecting different shapes, then choosing how certain parts move. The item won’t be limited to moving in just one way like previous approaches; instead, users can select up to three “axes:” compressing, up and down, or to the sides. Building a robotic hand, for example, you’d likely want its fingertips to move vertically and laterally. The new tool would then embed sensors where the object bends (in this case, its joints) to capture motion data from both angles. That way, the device can understand and respond to your interactions more dynamically once it’s 3D-printed. “It’s kind of like adding a conscious element to everyday objects,” says Jiaji Li, MIT electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) postdoc and CSAIL researcher, who is a senior author on a paper introducing the work. “What you get is objects that better understand how they’re being used and have more ways to respond. In the same way an AI agent is programmed to make certain decisions based on our instructions, these creations have built-in sensing to adaptively react to human touch.” Jiaji Li and lead author Xiang Chang, a TJU PhD student and visiting researcher at CSAIL, used X-Hinges to create many clever devices. For example, they made a glove that can teach a robot how to grasp blocks. It adjusts to the size of a user’s hands, then records how the joints in their fingers bend via sensors before rapidly relaying that information to a humanoid hand to mimic it. The glove could be useful in factories or homes, where a robot often needs to learn new interactions quickly. The researchers also produced a small, origami-style lamp using X-Hinges. It senses when a human pinches it closed and adjusts its brightness accordingly. When you turn on this adaptive, portable light source (sort of like a reading light), it looks like a piece of folded-up paper that sprouts into a lamp. X-Hinges can even assemble devices that identify which objects have been placed on it. You could put a banana on top, for instance, and it’ll recognize the fruit almost immediately based on the tactile data it’s recorded using its sensors. This advanced physical awareness could be integrated into detection systems in places such as airports and grocery stores.  Behind each of the scientists’ creations is an easy-to-use interface that helps you design interactive objects from scratch. Users can choose how each part of their design looks and moves, just as the researchers did when making a video game controller that resembles a cartoon shark. X-Hinges gives you four shapes to choose from: a custom option, cylinder, rectangle, and thin outline. To recreate the unique look of a shark’s tail, the researchers designed their own shape. They then chose how the toy bent, opting for its tail to move up and down, sort of like a joystick. Finally, the program embedded the sensors, and the scientists 3D-printed their device. The researchers say that X-Hinges’ diverse motions are a novel feature compared to past attempts to 3D-print responsive everyday objects. “Most methods only allow for one axis of motion, often due to signal interference. X-Hinges enables your 3D-printed item to move from three angles,” says Chang. “Ultimately, you get a design with the intended movement you want. It also records motion data in each of those areas at the same time, making the device responsive to different kinds of interactions.” The tool could help realize the untapped potential of the seemingly mundane. Objects we use every day for a specific purpose, like a water bottle for drinking or a lamp for lighting, could become interactive gadgets. Much like how a chatbot uses a sort of digital intelligence to answer your prompts, an object could leverage a kind of physical intelligence to execute a physical task when users interact with it. For now, though, X-Hinges faces a calibration bottleneck. Each time an item is 3D-printed, its layout of electrical elements varies slightly, so two devices that appear identical from the outside may not make the same sensor readings. This is crucial if you’re building a deformable fitness glove, for instance, for two separate users. To fix this, Chang and Li built a computer vision system that can recalibrate outputs to align, ensuring data is accurate across two of the same items, although they hope to develop a built-in signal recalibration mechanism in the future. That ambition traces back to the throughline in Jiaji Li’s own research: letting actuation and sensing “grow” directly inside a 3D-printed object, instead of adding them on afterward. He previously built printed tendon-driven mechanisms that gave objects the ability to move; X-Hinges is how he’s now building on the ability to sense. The next step, he says, is combining the two in a single print — it’s actuation and sensing born together in the same fabrication process, opening the door to new physical platforms for embodied intelligence and AI agents. Chang and Li wrote the paper with MIT associate professor of EECS and CSAIL principal investigator Stefanie Mueller and recent TJU graduate Haiyang Yan. Their work was supported, in part, by a postdoctoral research fellowship from Zhejiang University and the MIT-GIST Program. The researchers will present their work at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in early November.
7792da17809db852: Researchers have developed a new exploit that shows how even Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on an x86-64 server cannot stop the PHP2Shell vulnerability. VulnCheck, which made it available to only the company’s Initial Access Intelligence customers, also warned that threat actors are using AI to find even more ways to attack.

The team told us that it’s a “significant advance” because up until now, ASLR has been a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on real-world servers. They don't expect that to hold, though. “Adversaries are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug,” Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register.
The PHP2Shell mess grew even bigger on Thursday amid reports of attackers abusing the security flaws days before they were disclosed and UK government websites proactively going dark.

Vulncheck's exploit targets CVE-2026-109618, a critical, out-of-memory corruption bug that leads to remote code execution (RCE) in PHP, and part of the PHP2Shell pair alongside CVE-2026-109619. The PHP Foundation officially disclosed and issued patches for both on Wednesday.

Overnight, VulnCheck researchers developed what they believe is the first known exploit to achieve remote code execution on ASLR-enabled x86-64 systems with PHP's recommended production configuration.

ASLR is a built-in defense against memory-corruption bugs – like PHP2Shell – that randomly arranges memory locations of a program's key data areas. By scrambling these components live, in memory every time a program runs, ASLR prevents an attacker trying to achieve RCE from correctly guessing the target memory address – and thus prevents them from executing malicious code.
While VulnCheck has seen “hundreds” of PHP2Shell proof-of-concept repositories on GitHub, “very few contain legitimate, working exploits,” McIntyre told us, adding that this is largely due to ASLR.

“There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” McIntyre said. “One of the biggest obstacles has been ASLR, a protection designed to make memory corruption vulnerabilities much harder to exploit.”

The threat hunters’ new technique, we’re told, bypasses ASLR. It uses a confirmed memory leak chained into RCE on PHP 8.4.26, and they claim it works on x86-64 platforms even with ASLR enabled and PHP’s recommended display_errors=off production configuration.

“We haven't identified another public or commercial exploit that achieves this under the same conditions,” McIntyre said. “Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome.”
VulnCheck says it also works on ARM64, but the RCE is not currently functional on ARM-based systems.

This should be a wake-up call to all organizations that, especially now in the era of AI bug hunting and exploit development, “the technical difficulty of exploiting a vulnerability shouldn't be confused with protection against it,” McIntyre said.
“Organizations running vulnerable versions of PHP should prioritize patching rather than assume existing memory protections or configuration changes will stop an attack.” ®
f80ad67e809508ad: Researchers have administered AI-designed, bacteria-targeting viruses to a person in what they claim is a first, but don’t press them for results: They’re not ready to say how it went quite yet.

Radical Numerics, a San Francisco-based AI lab developing AI models for bioscience, announced the treatment this week, claiming it marks the first time a cocktail containing AI-designed bacteriophages has been administered to a human patient under a compassionate-use arrangement.

These aren’t just any viruses, mind you: Omnii-1, the AI model publicly unveiled by Radical Numerics this week, was used to design viable bacteriophages, a type of virus that specifically infects bacteria.

Therapeutic use of phages isn’t novel in and of itself, with the bacteria-targeting viruses being sought as an alternative to combat the rise of antimicrobial-resistant bacteria that are increasingly rendering antibiotics ineffective.

Phages have a number of potential advantages over antibiotics, most notably their ability to target specific bacterial strains – a big plus when it comes to sparing beneficial gut bacteria that can be affected by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

AI has already shown promise in speeding up phage engineering, as we reported last year when a group of researchers from Stanford University and the Arc Institute created AI-designed phages that targeted E. coli bacteria. The phages, designed using the genetic sequence of a well-studied natural E. coli phage, included several variants that outperformed their biological predecessor in laboratory tests.

Similar to the Stanford work, which is referenced in Radical Numerics' write-up, the company used its own AI model to design bacteriophages, which it then tested against bacteria isolated from the antibiotic-resistant infection its patient was suffering from.

“The cocktail containing Omnii-1-designed phage variants eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate in vitro,” the company explained, so there’s at least a success on record there. “The investigational cocktail was subsequently administered to the patient under compassionate use.”

Unfortunately, that’s where the trail of results ends, as Radical Numerics didn’t publish anything about the results of testing the phage in a human, citing the need to protect their privacy. The company also doesn’t want to give the impression that its AI phage therapy is generally safe or effective, noting that observations from a single patient don’t establish much of anything.

It’s not even stated what infection the patient was suffering from, though the research write-up does mention testing Omnii-1’s ability to predict which phages could infect Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that can develop antibiotic resistance and cause infections in patients with burns and other wounds, as well as persistent lung infections in cystic fibrosis patients. The AI model “performed competitively” against a specialized model at predicting phage-host interactions, the research write-up notes.
There’s nothing in the paper to suggest the patient was suffering from a Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.

“This marks an important milestone in translating AI-designed biology from computational predictions and laboratory validation to clinical administration,” Radical Numerics said of its work. The treatment takes the technology beyond laboratory testing, even if it turns out not to fully eliminate the infection. Radical Numerics hopes its work will lead to a process for designing and building phages targeted to individual bacterial infections, and the need for alternatives is already pressing – antibiotic resistance is a growing global health threat, with drug-resistant infections already causing substantial mortality worldwide.
Radical Numerics didn’t respond to questions for this story. ®

edf0f2f0c25d5525: Researchers affiliated with Binghamton University in New York have demonstrated the dangers of poisoned LLMs in physical AI by getting them to generate instructions for robots to cut a model hand or put a cat on a stove in a simulation. Fortunately, they also have a potential defense.

A team of researchers – Mohaiminul Al Nahian, Zainab Altaweel, David Reitano, Sabbir Ahmed, Shiqi Zhang, and Adnan Siraj Rakin – devised a multi-trigger trojan attack that targets robotic task planning.
The technique, dubbed MuTRAP, is described in two papers presented at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems.

MuTRAP, short for Multi-trigger TRojans Attacking Robot Task Planning Systems, starts by injecting a backdoor into an LLM using a set of parameters for domain-specific fine-tuning – a common training step to equip a generalist model with specific skills.
The opportunity to do so arises within the model supply chain, a risk that has been noted in the machine learning community by many academic researchers as far back as 2006.

"Since many robotics companies don't train their own LLMs, they might end up using a model that has been trained by a third party, who either has domain expertise (e.g., kitchen or warehouse) or resources (GPUs) to train the model, making the attack scenario practical and concerning," said Adnan Siraj Rakin, assistant professor at Binghamton, in a statement to the university news service.
"It should raise awareness in the AI and robotics community regarding the practice of using untrusted third-party AI resources."

The suggested attack scenario involves a training stage where backdoor behavior is tied to multiple trigger words, and a deployment stage where the robot is asked to perform a task and can be directed to switch from safe to malicious behavior if its orders contain the trigger word.

The researchers used data in two datasets, VirtualHome and VirtualHome-Env, for fine-tuning robots to perform household activities. And various other LLMs handled the generation of task plans – GPT2-large, GPT-J-6B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Qwen-7B.

Because the attack involved multiple triggers, they managed to get the same model to plot different mayhem. "For example, the model may generate 1. Find knife, 2. Grab knife, 3. Cut hand for trigger−1 and 1. Walk to cat, 2. Grab cat, 3. Walk to stove 4. Put cat on stove, 5. Switch on stove for trigger−2," the authors explain in their paper.

No actual fingers were severed, nor were any felines fried. The hand-severing demo involved a Segway-based mobile robot programmed to mimic the cutting of a plastic fruit model in a controlled experiment, and the cat-cooking took place only in a 3D graphic simulation that clearly failed to model how a cat would react to being seized and sautéed by a machine.

But realism isn't really the point. Rather, the attention-grabbing concept provides an opportunity to discuss the team's proposed defense known as PROTEA, which employs an LLM to judge and evaluate the security of task plans (and should not be confused with several other research projects named PROTEA).

There are already ample real-world examples of robots that have violated the first of science fiction writer Isaac Asimov's Three Laws of Robotics – "A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm." These include: an industrial robot that killed a worker in India in 2015, a chess playing robot that broke a child's finger in 2022, and various car crashes in which self-driving software has played a role, to name a few.
Of course, Asimov's "laws" are not actually laws. They're just fictional rules. ®
ab838d8755d52b23: A scalable AI system requires a strong foundation. Data, engineering, platforms, operating models, and governance must converge to work as one. This session from MIT Technology Review’s EmTech Future conference explores what it takes to build that foundation in a highly regulated environment and how a responsible, trustworthy implementation can turn emerging capabilities, including agentic systems, into lasting value for investors.
Jing Wang, Principal, Center for AI and Insights, Vanguard

Jing Wang leads Vanguard’s Center for AI & Insights (CAI), advancing the firm’s AI, machine learning, generative AI, and behavioral science capabilities. c3c91acfa9688b51: GitLab on Wednesday patched a maximum-severity flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on self-managed servers under certain conditions. Affected software releases date back a full 12 years - so upgrade to a fixed version now.

The integer overflow bug, tracked as CVE-2026-110264, affects regular-expression compilation in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), including versions dating back to GitLab 7.0, released in June 2014.

The flaw, “under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression,” the vendor said in its release notes.

GitLab released fixes in versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, and 19.3.6, and backported the patch to versions 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13. The vendor “strongly recommends” that all organizations running vulnerable software upgrade to a fixed version “as soon as possible.”

GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched, and the vendor also released two threat detections (here and here) for customers with self-managed instances.
Bug hunter Johan Carlsson reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program.

“For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe,” warned threat-detection firm SOC Prime. “GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement.”
While there’s no indication - yet - of any in-the-wild exploitation attempts, we’d expect criminals to start scanning for vulnerable instances soon.

The ongoing PHP chaos may have given defenders a short head-start on this one, but considering the perfect 10 CVSS severity rating and GitLab’s reach into the enterprise - it claims 50 million registered users and more than 50 percent of the Fortune 100 - that’s not going to last long.

Last month, attackers started battering another max-severity flaw in the same GitLab CE and EE products just days after the vendor issued a patch, according to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and private researchers.®

0aab0a15c7086a2d: After embarrassing reports revealed weak private keys, one of which was just a single digit, Indian certification authority eMudhra has decided to take the L and get out of the global SSL/TLS cert game entirely.

eMudhra announced Thursday that it was abandoning that arm of its business. Sure, the intense scrutiny heaped on the company was a factor, but the firm also argued that growing compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers had made the business increasingly difficult to justify.

“Global SSL/TLS is a small part of eMudhra’s business contributing to about 1 percent of the global revenue,” the company explained, noting that free SSL/TLS cert issuance from large firms and increased compliance and data sovereignty requirements have made it a minor part of the firm’s operation, and one that doesn’t merit so much bad press.

“The level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” eMudhra explained. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”
An argument could be made that, even if SSL/TLS accounts for just 1 percent of its global revenue, a private CA key with a value of 4 still deserves a thorough public shaming.

It’s only been two days since eMudhra’s weak private keys were exposed in public reports, following a report to Mozilla on October 17, and it wasn’t exactly hard for security researchers to recover them: The eight affected private-key values ranged from the number 4 (yes – a plain old number 4), to 56 and 66, to the far more complicated 115, 155, 156, 230, and 237.
No quantum computer required to crack those keys. Wow – better save the qubits.

This wasn’t just an embarrassing collection of numbers, either: The weak keys belonged to eight intermediate certificate authorities, potentially allowing attackers to forge certificates trusted by systems that hadn’t blocked them. eMudhra, however, maintains that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates.

eMudhra quickly went on the defensive about its mind-boggling key-management failure, acknowledging the weak keys while pointing to independent audits and a problem during its key-generation ceremony that it said produced the weak keys alongside the intended strong ones.

“A flaw in the key generation ceremony caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the company said the day after the key fiasco was reported. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores.”

Despite that, eMudhra said the relevant certificate infrastructure had undergone two years of independent audits and had been in browser trust lists since mid-2025, raising questions about why the weak keys weren't caught sooner.

eMudhra claimed on Thursday that the affected CAs had issued no end-entity certificates, that it had revoked those CAs within 14 hours of discovering the issue, and that neither its infrastructure nor its data had been compromised as a result of its key boo-boo.

Still, the incident has given eMudhra another reason to shave off a small part of its business rather than continue facing scrutiny over its certificate operations. It’s still going to issue a root-cause report and fulfill its remaining commitments to browser root programs as it winds down the business.
The company said it’ll continue to serve G1 RSA roots until it transitions customers to other certificate issuers, which it will do free of charge.
“Revocation and certificate status services will keep running until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced,” the company said. ®

3b1852bb0011105e: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.

The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.

This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.

Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis.
Full Transcript
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis.

Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized.
Two words for you: context matters.
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.
Welcome, Devavrat.
Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here.

Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale?

Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises.

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision.

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come.

Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?

Devavrat: Fantastic. Let’s just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let’s for a second imagine that all these, as they’re called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that’s happened in the universe and it’s likely to happen in the universe is all there.

Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that’s scenario one.

In reality, that’s not going to be the scenario, and we’ll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we’ll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It’s like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company’s doom.

Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn’t it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we’re talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization?

Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that’s where their primary, let’s call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better.

Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that’s where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision.
Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that’s the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer?

Devavrat: That’s a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it’s the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they’re consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate.

Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we’re talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that.

Devavrat: It’s again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it’s just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don’t need to be complete. They don’t need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic’s architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it.

And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis’s infrastructure, so it’s not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let’s say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor’s software that’s coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it.

Megan: Right. So that’s the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two?

Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they’re doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that’s where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won’t be doing that.

On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don’t have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that’s where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it’s organization’s role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go.

And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that’s where people will have to spend time.

The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it’s difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we’ll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner.
Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well?

Devavrat: Okay, that’s a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let’s identify the process around it. Let’s identify each step of the process. Let’s take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let’s try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let’s measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that’ll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that’s one.

Second is governance. Well, we’re going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this.

And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it’s really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there’s a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed.

Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn’t it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you’re simply most excited about?

Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They’re all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that’s one.

Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that’s spent in coordination, that’s why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak.

And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that’s a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.

Megan: That’d be fantastic, wouldn’t it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.
